#9095. Finnegan Shannon installs conveyor belt for displaying art accessibly in Brooklyn

New York City-based artist Finnegan Shannon has installed a conveyor belt to display art at cultural centre Pioneer Works in Brooklyn, USA, as a commentary on accessibility in art.

According to Pioneer Works, the There’s No Me Without You installation fulfils Shannon’s “longtime fantasy of an exhibition space that would meet their access needs”.

Chairs were placed around the closed-loop 12-foot-long mechanism, letting visitors sit when viewing and engaging with exhibited objects, archival materials and portable DVD players placed on a series of moving trays.

It was created from a restaurant-style system similar to those used in sushi restaurants where the food is delivered via a conveyor belt. The rest of the room on the upper floor of the arts centre was covered in rich fabrics and built-in benches along the perimeter.

“My conveyor belt, technically a retail and restaurant-style display system, is a tool for me to be in less pain when I’m experiencing art,” said Shannon, who is disabled. “I notice I am a much more patient and curious visitor when I’m sitting down.”

The title of the installation reflects the artist’s relationship to the concept of interdependence.

“If disabled people were in charge, we would have a bunch of varied and deluxe options for sitting and lying down in exhibition spaces,” they said.

“Instead we live in a world where this type of infrastructure is quite basic and sparse.”

The installation is being used to present new commissions by artists with disabilities Joselia Rebekah Hughes, Ariana Martinez and Alex Dolores Salerno. For the three consecutive exhibitions, visitors are invited to interact with the work through touch, sight, and sound.

Air filters with bright colours were included in the middle of the conveyor belt to assist with air quality and masks were encouraged for visitors.

Shannon emphasised the collaborative nature of artistic endeavour through the exhibition.

“We know that on some fundamental level, no solo exhibition is truly a solo endeavor,” Shannon said.

“Putting together an exhibition takes immense collaboration and support – art handlers, facilities staff, curators, registrars, accountants, assistants – and that is all within the institution.”

“You can trace that entanglement further: I’m dependent on workers, paid and unpaid care labor, and friendships, family, and more, both locally and across the globe.”

“I never want someone to come away from an exhibition with my work feeling like they’ve experienced something that is mine,” they said. “Instead I hope they have threads to follow to learn more about the vast world of knowledge that is disability culture.”

Shannon’s other projects have focused on access. Alt Text as Poetry, a collaboration with Bojana Coklyat exploring image description and Do You Want Us Here or Not is a series of museum benches and cushions designed to encourage rest.

Other designs that prioritise accessibility were showcased at The Fashion Institute of Technology’s Adapt/Evolve exhibition in New York last year.

There’s No Me Without You is on show at Pioneer Works in Brooklyn from 12 September to 20 December. For more exhibitions, installations and talks worldwide, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

#9093. Shure’s New MV360 Mics Promise to Make Spatial Audio Capture Easier

Shure’s New MV360 Mics Promise to Make Spatial Audio Capture Easier

Shure is entering the increasingly crowded spatial audio market with its new MV360 microphones.

Just last week, Blackmagic Design unveiled the Ambisonic Microphone, a high-end studio solution. Last month, Sony arrived on the scene with its ECM-AX10, a $250 spatial audio mic for content creators. Built with creators in mind, Shure’s new $349 USB-C MV360 is much closer to Sony’s offering in both price and functionality.

Shure says its new MV360 “makes immersive audio more accessible to creators at every level.” To achieve this, the plug-and-play mic features ready-to-use Capture Modes, including immersive binaural, stereo, mono, and auto-tracking.

The mono and stereo modes are self-explanatory, working just as they would on a traditional mic. Immersive binaural promises a broader, more lifelike soundstage, which Shure says is ideal for headphone playback. Meanwhile, auto-tracking mode focuses the virtual microphone toward the loudest sound source, such as a speaker in an interview or podcast.

Each Capture Mode records a ready-to-use two-channel file that requires no post-production. However, creators who opt for full 360-degree recording gain significantly more flexibility, as they can edit the Ambisonic B-format (Ambix) file in Shure’s Motiv software or compatible third-party apps.

As Shure explains, the MV360 captures a stronger sense of place than a traditional microphone.

“Listeners can feel closer to a podcast conversation, more immersed in an ASMR scene, or transported into the middle of a bustling market or quiet forest,” Shure says.

The MV360 is a relatively compact spatial microphone housed in an all-metal body. It records and draws power over a single USB-C cable, ensuring compatibility with a wide range of devices, including smartphones and many cameras. Alongside Shure’s Motiv apps, the MV360 supports various third-party applications, allowing users to record 360-degree audio directly to Motiv or a DAW of their choice.

“Sound can make the difference between watching a moment and feeling part of it,” says Eduardo Valdes, Associate Vice President of Global Marketing and Product Management at Shure.

“Until now, capturing that sense of presence has required expensive equipment, technical expertise and time that many creators simply don’t have. The MV360 changes that. It gives creators an easy way to bring listeners closer to the conversation, the performance or the world around them, while giving experienced professionals the control they need to shape every detail,” Valdes continues.

The Shure MV360 is available now for $349 and includes the USB-C mic, a small tripod, cold shoe mic clip, phone clamp, extra cables, carrying case, and windscreen.

Alongside the standard model, Shure also unveiled the MV360+ today, slated to arrive in early 2027. Designed for field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers, the MV360+ works with mirrorless cameras, DSLRs, action cameras, 360-degree cameras, and more. It also adds onboard 32-bit float and internal recording capabilities, a rechargeable battery, and wireless control functionality.

The Shure MV360+ will retail for $449 when it arrives early next year.

#9091. Panasonic Lumix SHX1 Review: The S1 II in Boxy Clothes

Panasonic Lumix SHX1 Review: The S1 II in Boxy Clothes

When the Panasonic S1 II was announced, one of my first thoughts was, “How are they going to top this with an S1H II?” The answer was, they didn’t. Instead, Panasonic is bringing the internals of the S1 II to a new form factor, a cinema box camera, and calling it the SHX1 ($4,699).If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II. PetaPixel Score 7.5/10 ProsClass leading image stabilization never seen in this style of cameraFantastic image quality with minimal rolling shutterExtremely modifiable designConsNo internal BRAW (requires an SSD)Some buttons feel mushy and are difficult to pressNo internal ND filter This is definitely not the FX5 competitor many were waiting for, but it still might make a lot of cinematographers and videographers very happy.

If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

Note that throughout this review I will be referring to this camera in comparison to the Panasonic S1 II. If you are unfamiliar with that camera, you can check out our review here. As well, as the SHX1 does not offer any stills capture, this review will be entirely focused on video capture.

The SHX1 is quite compact for a cinema camera, similar to a RED Komodo and weighing only 948 grams (33.4 ounces). In a departure from Panasonic’s previous BG-Series box cameras, this SHX1 includes a top-mounted LCD monitor, with extensive 4-axis articulation and 1.84M dots of resolution.

The articulation is extremely useful, as you can shoot above your eye-line, something usually prohibited with top-mounted displays. There are dedicated exposure buttons on the body, as well as Menu, Back and AF-On. These buttons have a pretty unresponsive feel to them, with little haptic feedback to let you know you’ve actually pushed the button. These can be customized, something I recommend to avoid excessive menu diving.

As expected for a cinema camera, the top, right side and bottom of the camera have plentiful 1/4-inch mounting points for rigs and accessories. The camera is powered by Mini V-Mount batteries, most of which are the same height as the camera. There is an active fan system in the body, which allows even 4K/120p footage to be captured indefinitely.

It’s worth pointing out that you can also purchase the SHX1 with an accessory kit ($5,499), which includes a top handle, XLR adapter and a side grip. The grip feels fantastic but is quite large. I consider it almost a necessary accessory, and the extra controls give operators several more options for custom buttons and a joystick for selecting the autofocus point. The top handle is very sturdy, and the removable XLR adapter gives you easily accessed gain controls. Unlike previous S-Series bodies, which relied on an XLR adapter to capture 32-bit float audio, the SHX1 can record 32-bit audio through the 3.5mm jacks and internal mic as well.

Footage can be stored on a UHS-II SD card, CFexpress Type B card, or external SSD. As expected with a cinema camera, there are locking ports for SDI video, timecode, and a full-size HDMI port. For further external control, a Live Production Unit called the AU-LPU1 will be released in early 2027.

The lack of built-in ND filters is a disappointment, but that was the compromise Panasonic was forced into when keeping the body so small. Screw-in filters or a matte box will be required for controlling light levels.

The sensor is the same full-frame 24.5MP partially stacked unit we saw in the S1 II, which is capable of outstanding results and well-controlled rolling shutter. The only difference is an anti-aliasing filter has been added to minimize incidents of moiré in finely detailed textures.

In my testing, though, I found very similar results to the S1 II, with neither camera giving me moiré even when shooting fabrics at moderate distance.

Like the S1 II, the SHX1 has a massive number of recording resolutions, frame shapes and frame rates. The headline feature is 6K Open Gate recording up to 30P, and 5.1K Open Gate using the full sensor up to 60P. For slow motion, the camera can capture 4K at up to 120P with sound. There is also the option to expand the dynamic range by reducing the readout speed. This does produce appreciably cleaner shadows, but with a corresponding increase in rolling shutter artifacts.

Video can be recorded with MP4, MOV and ProRes codecs for standard 10-bit video. There is also the option to capture 12-bit RAW video in either ProRes RAW or BRAW flavours. Bafflingly, though only ProRes RAW can be recorded to the CFexpress card, BRAW requires an external SSD. This is particularly odd as BRAW offers extremely efficient 12:1 compression rates, which could be easily written to a card. Adding insult to injury, the camera’s startup time is dramatically increased with an SSD attached, taking nearly 10 seconds and often leading to me missing shots.

The video quality itself from the camera is outstanding, with impressive detail and expansive dynamic range even when Dynamic Range Boost is not active. Log video can be captured in either Panasonic V-Log gamma or ARRI’s LogC3. The Panasonic V-Log gamma remains my favourite log curve to work with, but ARRI’s gamma is very flexible and the industry standard in the filmmaking world.

What sets the video quality from the SHX1 apart from any other box camera is the inclusion of incredibly effective in-body image stabilization, based on the S1 II system. This works great in its default mode, but even better when Panasonic lenses are attached and the “Cropless” stabilization is engaged. The camera’s autofocus abilities are also quite reliable, though perhaps not quite as rock-solid as Sony’s and Canon’s more recent implementations. Humans and animals can be automatically detected, and there is a good degree of “stickiness” when following moving subjects.

If you don’t require the box-camera form factor, then the SHX1 can be a confusing proposition. The S1 II features nearly all of the video capabilities with excellent photography specs and an EVF in a considerably more affordable package.

However, many professional videographers and cinematographers require the box-camera design to make it easy to build rigs or mount the camera in a variety of locations. The forthcoming Live Production Unit will add further versatility for using the SHX1 as a remote camera, something the S1 II cannot offer.

As well, if absolute reliability is important, the more robust cooling system in the SHX1 means overheating will not be a concern even when recording demanding footage in hot areas. The S1 II has very good thermals for a hybrid mirrorless camera, but in professional situations absolute reliability is imperative.

Compact cinema cameras like the RED Komodo-X 6K ($4,995) and Blackmagic Pyxis 6K ($2,249) offer similar form factors and outstanding image quality. Unlike the SHX1, these can record extremely compressed RAW video internally. However, the autofocus performance is vastly behind the SHX1, and neither offers IBIS. RED and Blackmagic may offer more bang for the buck for filmmakers, but the SHX1 is the clear choice for handheld documentary work.

RED Komodo-X 6KBuy new on B&HRED Komodo-X 6KBuy used on KEH.comBlackmagic Pyxis 6KBuy new on B&HBlackmagic Pyxis 6KBuy used on KEH.com

The Sony FX5 is also a compact full-frame cinema camera with great autofocus and IBIS. The FX5 can accept an optional EVF, has more reliable autofocus and records compressed X-OCN RAW video internally. However, the SHX1 features much more effective stabilization and industry-standard connections. For event work, the Sony makes more sense, whereas the Panasonic will find itself more at home in commercial environments.

Maybe. If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

#9089. Xiaomi’s Eye-Catching Pro Series Phones Go Global for the First Time

Xiaomi’s Eye-Catching Pro Series Phones Go Global for the First Time

Xiaomi officially released its 18 Pro Series phones, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, at a launch event in Paris, marking the first time it’s pushing its Pro models outside of China. That also makes them outliers in another respect: they are rare slab smartphones with two displays.

Both will hit select markets — not North America — in the coming weeks and months and carry on Xiaomi’s existing partnership with Leica as camera-centric devices. They also feature a rear LTPO AMOLED screen positioned as a creative tool for those who like selfies but want more variety.

Xiaomi already foreshadowed this launch when unveiling the devices at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September 2026, so specs, especially on the camera side, weren’t entirely a mystery. Once they launched in China shortly afterward, the cat was pretty much out of the bag.

We know the main differences between the two phones have to do with screen size, image sensors, the Snapdragon chip, and battery capacity. The 18 Pro Max gets a larger 6.9-inch LTPO AMOLED display (2624 x 1208) with Xiaomi’s own Shield Glass protection, a 1-120Hz variable refresh rate, 4,000 nits of peak brightness, and BT.2020 support. It also runs on the more powerful Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite Extreme chipset and packs a 7,050mAh battery.

Otherwise, the Pro has a smaller 6.4-inch panel (2436 x 1120) with the same display specs as its Max sibling. It also steps down a bit, running on the Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite chip, and, given its smaller size, has a 6,000mAh battery.

There are slight differences in the rear display size, as the 18 Pro Max features a larger 2.9-inch panel compared to the 2.7-inch screen on the 18 Pro. Both will come with 12GB of RAM and 256GB or 512GB storage configurations, though the Pro Max also offers a 16GB RAM and 1TB storage variant.

Interestingly, Xiaomi equips both phones with almost the exact same camera specs. The three Leica-branded rear cameras are largely identical on both models, with one key exception: the 18 Pro Max uses the LOFIC-equipped Light Fusion 960L sensor, whereas the 18 Pro uses the standard Light Fusion 960.

The 200-megapixel main camera (23mm equivalent) uses a Type 1/1.28 Light Fusion 960L image sensor and an f/1.67 aperture. Thanks to LOFIC technology, it delivers better dynamic range than both a standard sensor and the 18 Pro’s main camera. You can tell just by pointing both phones at any subject before even snapping the shutter. There’s also optical image stabilization with a CIPA-rated seven stops of shake correction. The Leica Summilux-designed lenses combine precision glass and plastic elements with what appears to be a glare-resistant coating.

The 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera (75mm equivalent) uses a Type 1/1.56 image sensor, an f/2.4 aperture, and 3.2x optical zoom. Finally, there’s the 50-megapixel ultra-wide camera, whose sensor size remains a mystery. It is somewhat of an outlier in that it’s a 17mm equivalent with a 102° field of view, which is noticeably narrower than most ultra-wide cameras on other phones.

On the software side, Xiaomi adds a new mode called Essential Moment that marries Leica color science with AI-driven image processing to emulate classic film and camera looks. Names like “B&W Film,” “Modern Vintage,” and “Iconic CCD” don’t specify exactly what stock they’re based on, but the new styles add a distinctly Xiaomi-infused element to the camera interface.

This is how Xiaomi frames it: “B&W Film captures the depth and tonal range of classic monochrome photography, Iconic CCD recreates the vivid, saturated colors of CCD-era digital cameras, and Modern Vintage offers refined tones with natural detail for a timeless look. Users can also replicate the optical characteristics of two classic lenses — a 35mm Documentary lens and a 75mm Portrait lens with soft bokeh.”

There are some unusual limitations, however. Pro mode doesn’t allow users to shoot in RAW at 50 megapixels, and there is still no 24fps option for video, including in Pro Video. None of the Leica styles and filters introduced in the Leitzphone by Xiaomi have migrated over to these devices, so you retain the same choices offered in other Xiaomi models.

The Back Display offers a fairly high degree of access to the overall camera interface, including modes, settings, customizations, and more. Xiaomi limits zoom to 0.7x and 1x, meaning there is no way to activate the telephoto camera, though the settings still let you hold up a palm to trigger the shutter hands-free.

While the live preview occupies a sizable portion of the display, Xiaomi configured it to light up in bright white elsewhere to help illuminate subjects in dimmer conditions. It limits available modes to Photo, Video, Portrait, and a retro-style option called Photo Booth, and strangely omits Leica filters from the equation (though you can still choose between Leica Authentic and Vibrant as the overarching style).

You also get the choice to shoot pixel-binned 12.5-megapixel or 50-megapixel stills, with video resolution options ranging from 720p all the way to 8K at either 30 or 60fps. Dolby Vision and a Teleprompter are also available as optional features.

It’s a fully functional display in that it works with swipes and gestures just as the main display does. Tap-to-focus works, as does focus tracking when double-tapping on yourself or another subject in the frame. You can preview shots you’ve taken and either press the onscreen shutter or use the volume buttons to capture a photo or video.

Since the screen uses the rear cameras, the dynamic range advantages apply equally; Xiaomi doesn’t appear to neuter the experience by dialing things back, particularly with the LOFIC sensor on the 18 Pro Max.

An added benefit of the Back Display is that it also works with notifications and real-time information, like calls, maps, ride-hailing, food delivery, audio recording, and more. Pin to Back Display allows you to pin text and images to it for quick reference, such as a boarding pass or QR code. There’s also the option to apply a different wallpaper to it, if you want.

Neither Xiaomi nor Leica made any mention of a photography or teleconverter lens kit for either phone, even as Xiaomi’s Chinese competitors continue to release more of them. There are possibilities there, but you would need a third-party setup to make it work. Thus far, Xiaomi has only made photography kits for its Ultra line, which it maintains is still the company’s flagship with a more specialized photography slant.

You won’t find the Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max in Canada or the U.S. unless you import them yourself. They’re both compatible with North American cellular networks, so there isn’t a hardware limitation in that regard. Warranty challenges aside, Xiaomi is offering five years of Android updates and six years of security updates.

Both models will come in the same four color variants: Black, White, Velvet Red, and Cosmic Blue. As for pricing, the Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at €1,399, while the 18 Pro Max starts at €1,599.

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date]."

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice says never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?"

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the issue your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

#9085. ‘It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person’: Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

Shafeena Yusuff Ali, who has master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact, set up Rizq Art Initiative in 2023 Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative

If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative

“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she says. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali says. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”

Informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she says.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”

As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

Shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

#9084. Pablo Castillo partners with Decibel on 3D-printed chair with under-seat storage

A bookshelf slots in below the cantilevered seat of Kino, a 3D-printed chair developed by Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo.

Castillo designed Kino for Decibel, an American company that specialises in 3D-printed furniture and installations. It is shortlisted for seating design of the year in the upcoming Dezeen Awards.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

The chair is essentially a monobloc, with a single component forming the T-shaped seat, two legs, the shelf and a curved backrest.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

Decibal also offers an outdoor version printed from recycled PETG, a thermoplastic polyester.

“I wanted the substantial thickness of the plastic and the way it builds a product layer by layer to translate into features that give the chair its character,” Castillo told Dezeen.

“Following this line of thought allowed me to move beyond mere dimensions and general ergonomic considerations,” the designer said.

“The cantilevered seat, the under-seat storage, and specific details such as the T-junctions naturally emerged.”

The seat’s T-shape was created by cantilevers both forwards and backwards. This makes the chair less rigid than a typical 3D-printed chair, improving comfort.

“By reinforcing the lower part of the seat with a corrugated structure integrated directly into the 3D print, we achieved a chair that offers a slightly broader range of motion than a traditional design,” Castillo said.

“It seamlessly accommodates highly reclined, relaxed postures, as well as more active positions when the user leans forward.”

Kino joins Decibel’s Editions collection, which also includes chairs by designers including Charles Birshaw, Karim Rashid and Deniz Aktay.

The New Jersey-based brand launched this collection with an exhibition at the Alcova show in Milan in 2025, when it was live-printing chairs in the former SNIA factory in Varedo.

The chairs are produced using a Caracol robotic 3D printer, which allows geometries that wouldn’t be possible with injection moulding.

#9083. The First Known Photograph of Bogotá Sold for Over $331K at Auction

The First Known Photograph of Bogotá Sold for Over $331K at Auction

The earliest known photograph of Bogotá, the capital of Colombia, taken in 1842, has sold for $331,600 at auction.

The daguerreotype, titled Rue de l’Observatoire, was sold by Christie’s this week as part of an auction of 350 photographs from the Roger Therond Collection: A French Passion. Roger Therond, was a journalist who served as editor of Paris Match for half a century and spent decades building a collection that brings together major works from the history of French photography.

This image, captured by French diplomat Jean-Baptiste Louis Gros, is not only one of the earliest known photographs of Colombia, but also one of the very first urban daguerreotypes made outside Europe and the United States.

It had been initially listed by Christie’s with an estimated value of up to $89,000, but the photograph far exceeded expectations, selling for nearly four times its estimated value.

The historic daguerreotype shows a nearly deserted street in the Colombian capital with the Andes mountains in the background.

Appointed chargé d’affaires in New Granada (present-day Colombia) in 1838, French diplomat Baron Gros was also a painter and draftsman. Shortly after the daguerreotype was publicly announced in 1839, he began experimenting with the new photographic process in the country. France had made the invention publicly available to encourage its spread around the world. News of the invention was published in the local newspaper El Observador on September 22, 1839. Gros was among the early travelers who recognized the potential of photography as a way to document places, record information, and represent the world around them.

“Photography in those days was, after all, the preserve of an elite; not everyone could afford the equipment,” Élodie Morel-Bazin, the European Head of Photography at Christie’s, tells Reuters. “He was a diplomat; he travelled a great deal; he probably came from a very distinguished family and had the means to devote himself to it. That was his hobby.”

Christie’s says the photograph is particularly remarkable for its 47-second exposure time. Its subject, a view of a city street, was also unusual for the period, when most photographs were portraits. The long exposure meant that people moving through the street were unlikely to appear in the image, leaving the city looking almost empty. The level of detail captured on the metal plate is remarkable, with the Andes mountains visible in the background. The auction house notes that photographing such distant features was technically challenging because haze and diffused light often obscured them.

#9082. Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the 'turbulence and violence of our times'

“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” says Tarini Malik, the curator of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section Sarah Bates

Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.

Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.

Curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.

“The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik says. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”

With Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.

The Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.

“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik says. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”

These themes, Malik says, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.

Through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.

With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.

The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.

“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik says. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”

The Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.

The Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.

Finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.

“We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik says. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”

All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik says, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.

“I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik says. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”

#9081. Texas antique and design show unveils new exhibition building made from salvaged materials

Photography by Marburger Farm and Ethan Good Photography

Texas-based antique and design show Marburger Farm has unveiled an exhibition building made partly from salvaged materials sourced directly from across the 43-acre property, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen.

Called Gage Hall, the building’s facade is made from reclaimed timber sourced from around the farm and is topped with a traditional Texas metal roof and contemporary skylight elements that bring natural light into the hall.

The hall brings an additional 7,500 square feet of shopping space to Marburger Farm, bringing the fair’s total space to 100,000 square feet. Designed to honour the site’s dairy farm heritage, the hall also showcases its vision for the future.

The antique and design show has become a destination for international designers looking to source unique interior objects including furniture, lighting and vintage textiles.

The 43-acre show is located in Round Top, Texas, and has attracted designers such as Kelly Wearstler and Leanne Ford.

The fair offers visitors access to objects from over 200 independent dealers and has become one of the largest antique shows in the United States.

The site also includes a Texas-style town square, 10 restored historic buildings, four tents and a 150-year-old saloon, which has been restored to its original use as a social space and bar.

Founded in 1997, the show has grown to attract over 30,000 people annually.

The antique show takes place in January, March and October each year.

Marburger Farm is owned by Brook Partners, a Dallas-based investment company focusing on culture and commerce.

The company also runs the upcoming Dallas Art Fair, which is held from 15 to 18 April 2027 in Dallas, Texas. To learn more, visit the Marburger Farm website.

Marburger Farm Antique Show took place from 27 to 31 October in Round Top, Texas. The winter show will take place 21-24 January and the spring show will take place 23-27 March 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

How do you make a branching game feel like a TV show? AdHoc’s co-founders explain, from recording Aaron Paul’s cast in conversation to ditching Telltale’s habits.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dispatch looks, sounds, and plays like an animated TV show, and that was deliberate: AdHoc wanted it to be a no-barrier entry point for people who don't usually play games. A year after its launch on 22 October 2025, the episodic superhero workplace comedy has more than five million players, and the new Dispatch Deluxe Edition offers new ways to play, including replacing its graphics with storyboard art.

The game stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as Robert Robertson, a former hero turned dispatcher for a team of reformed supervillains, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast. Getting that cast to feel like they're in the same room, and getting the player to feel part of the story, took a lot of invisible work.

You can read how four video tracks and a doughnut shop gave Dispatch its start, but here I ask co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO, and both co-creative directors, how they nailed down the premium animation.

How do you keep dialogue, facial expressions and performances consistent when the player can send a scene in different directions? While it was made using Unreal Engine 5, it starts on the page. "Everything is written with choice in mind," says Herman.

AdHoc built its own tools to ingest scripts, including a playable script you can read and click through. That produces the recording script actors use in the booth, which Herman says is "a little bit crazy to read on a linear page". Do it long enough, though, and it starts to make sense. Each scene has a spine, and every time a choice appears, different options eventually trunk back into the main flow.

The studio also uses recordings as a directing tool. AdHoc ingests every performance as it’s captured, so when an actor records opposite someone already in the booth, the team can play those existing lines back for them to react to. In Herman’s example, with Aaron Paul already recorded, the team can bring in Erin as Blonde Blazer, play Paul’s lines for her to read off, then play him again after her response. It’s a clever bit of craft: AdHoc builds each conversation around real delivery. The effect, Herman says, is to simulate the actors being in the same room, which helps performances feel grounded and integrated. It also gives a scene its flow, because the actors know where they’re coming in from, and it makes testing branches easy.

It's clever craft. Rather than recording actors in isolation and hoping the performances fit together later, AdHoc builds the conversation around real delivery. The effect, Herman says, is to simulate the actors being in the same room, which helps performances feel grounded and integrated. It also gives a scene its flow, because the actors know where they're coming in from, and it makes testing branches easy.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

By the time animation begins, the voice work is trusted, and the team is happy with it. The facial animation then comes down to knowing every character. "Not everyone laughs the same. When they cry, they look different," Herman says. "Every character is their own person. Like they are on the page, they are in animation." Getting there takes "a lot of review, a lot of ref", and the team shoots plenty of reference footage for its animators.

For AdHoc, the problem was the seam: the point where a cutscene ends and gameplay begins. “The goal was always to make it feel integrated,” Lenart says. Part of the studio’s philosophy is that gameplay and story should feel like a seamless handoff rather than two different experiences. He and Herman had worked on plenty of games with clear story sections and clear gameplay sections, “and you could feel that break every single time”. That, he says, “always kind of drove us crazy”.

When they dreamed of starting their own studio, one mandate was to choose mechanics that feel like an integrated part of a character's life, not scenes contrived for interactivity. If someone has to break into a room and pick a lock, it shouldn't be something the character would never do.

For Dispatch, that meant the shift mechanic. Robert sends heroes out on calls because it's his job. "It's the thing he does every day," says Lenart. "So, when he sits down at his computer to do it, it feels natural."

The team also made sure the Z-Team keep talking to the player throughout each shift, so the dialogue and relationships keep flowing, and the story never stops for gameplay. At times, a shift cuts out to a cinematic and back in again, and Lenart says that only feels organic because "we spent a lot of time and effort to make it that way".

Herman and Lenart both spent years at Telltale Games, the studio behind The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderlands, and Dispatch forced them to drop much of their old way of working.

At Telltale, Lenart says, cinematics were "fast and loose". Episodes were made in what the studio called live development: they would release one episode, then spend the next six weeks on the following. Things "could change at any time". Player feedback from the previous episode could feed straight back in, with tweaks to cinematics and character intentions right up until the day before shipping.

Dispatch had a different goal. AdHoc wanted the visuals and style to feel like "a premium animated television show" that wasn't a barrier for people who might enjoy a story like this but aren't typically into games. That meant a more traditional animation pipeline, with decisions made much earlier and, in some cases, locked down a year in advance.

"That was a really big learning curve for us since we were used to being able to make small adjustments all the way up until the last minute," Lenart says. But he now thinks the discipline made the game better. It "forced many detailed conversations way earlier in the process, which only better informed how each piece of the story was going to play out". His verdict: "Oh, this is actually the way to make the best quality product."

The Dispatch Deluxe Edition is out now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch / Switch 2, and $10.99 digital upgrade path for existing owners

#9077. Gen Z apps inform approachable wayfinding for V&A East Storehouse

On a mission to draw in museum sceptics, Hackney design studio Fieldwork Facility looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating the Dezeen Award-shortlisted wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse.

The landmark museum, completed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro last May, has been lauded for opening up the V&A‘s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects, to the public for the first time.

The challenge for Fieldwork Facility was to help visitors navigate and interpret this trove of artefacts – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

To speak to this demographic, studio founder Robin Howie decided to borrow a visual language they’re already intimately familiar with.

“We studied popular Gen-Z apps and services to understand how to make Storehouse feel intuitive as soon as you walk through the door,” Howie told Dezeen.

“Cultural institutions can all too often feel like exclusive environments with many barriers to entry. It’s unfortunately far too easy for so many people to walk into a museum, gallery or national organisation and feel a queasy sense of ‘this isn’t really for me’.”

As an antidote, Howie and his team decided to treat the wayfinding design like an operating system in itself, looking to the UX of much-used apps like TikTok to inform signage and interaction points across the museum.

From the get-go, visitors are welcomed with an “onboarding text” that introduces them to the Storehouse and how to navigate it.

“It’s a moment that purposefully feels like opening an app for the first time where you are given a quick orientation of the experience held inside,” said Howie.

The text combines a range of different media, including printed typography, ticker tape screens and recycled paper tiles.

Topped with recycled plastic letterforms, these tiles provide a first introduction to three key colours used to mark different areas across the building.

Yellow points out viewing galleries, green is for the museum’s viewable restoration labs and pink for the Study Centre, which gives the public unprecedented access to the collection through the V&A’s Order an Object programme – a service traditionally reserved for researchers and academics.

Set into aluminium cases, these recycled paper tiles were used to form adaptable, modular signage across the building. Much like a Scrabble tile, each is emblazoned with a single letter, allowing museum staff to adapt the wayfinding based on what objects are currently on view.

“Storehouse’s signage system looks and feels programmable in an analogue way,” said Howie.

To suit the use across separate tiles, Fieldwork Facility commissioned a bespoke version of the V&A’s brand typeface Spiller that is monospaced.

This technique, normally used for typesetting computer code, involves shaping each letter so it occupies the same amount of horizontal space.

“The resulting Spiller Mono helps give V&A East its own unique language that is atypical for a museum,” Howie said.

“We also love that monospace typefaces were widely used in early computers and are still standard for writing and editing code – great nod to the ‘building as software’ concept.”

On some signs, a colourful, enamelled lava-stone disc provides colour coding, echoing the yellow, green and pink first introduced in the onboarding text.

Several other interventions were also designed to encourage interaction, either from visitors or from staff, who engage with the building both as a museum and an active storehouse.

To provide museumgoers with context and explanation about the pieces on show, Fieldwork Facility created interpretation labels that exist as a modular kit of components, allowing them to be fixed to Storehouse’s standardised crates, palettes and forklift-accessible shelving. Digital templates allow staff to amend these labels without relying on the designers.

The design studio even introduced dedicated “expression points” where visitors can share their opinion with the V&A staff or take part in public polls using a voting coin system.

“The operating system approach welcomes everyone to explore, define their own experience, make connections and have agency within a national institution,” Howie said.

All of the museum’s signage was designed to be adapted and reused to cut out waste, with icons for permanent fixtures – such as toilets, elevators and floor numbers – screen printed or painted directly onto the walls instead of relying on disposable vinyl decals.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphics for V&A Storehouse East have been shortlisted for graphic design of the year at the 2026 Dezeen Awards. It is up against seven other projects, including the visual identity for Dorte Mandrup’s Arctic whale watching facility and ink-free tea packaging for a Song Dynasty-themed restaurant in Guangzhou.

#9076. Special Edition: Jesus

Mona Chalabi, Anne Anlin Cheng and Patty Chang, Miles Greenberg, Betsy James Wyeth, and the hottest memes about the Nvidia honeypot.

Framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.

In the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the issue as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago.

Down the street, a place that pretended to be a legitimate art gallery for a couple of months, showing the worst possible commercial art, has finally given up, and now it’s selling fur coats. A man in a cowboy hat walks past two girls dancing for a social media video. The air is chilly, and I think of buying myself a leather jacket.

She looks at me with the most loving eyes as she holds a stack of perfectly folded laundry. She comforts me with her wide, auspicious smile, her jet-black hair, and her wrinkle-free, porcelain skin. I feel safe, accepted, and not judged. “Fast service, same day,” she promises because she’s just a model in an ad for a laundromat.

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026). | Lakshmi Rivera Amin

$100 off makes the 2026 iPad Air great value.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black Friday iPad deals are already coming in, with early discounts on most models as the holidays approach. But, having tracked iPad Black Friday prices for close to a decade, I'd hold off buying for now in all but one case: Amazon's $100 off the M4 iPad Air.

With iPad prices inevitably more expensive than during Black Friday last year because of RAM and SSD shortages, this could be as good a deal as we get on the latest Air, and it offers pretty good value. If you do need more power, up to $150 off the M5 iPad Pro at B&H Photo is also tempting. But I think the lower-spec iPads could still fall in price as Black Friday gets closer.

If you need help deciding which iPad to choose, our expert guides to the iPad generations and the best iPad for drawing are the places to turn to.

This is a decent if not spectacular deal on the entry configuration of the 11-inch Pro. B&H also has $100 off the larger 13-inch iPad Pro which we gave 4.5 stars, and up to $150 off the 512GB SSD configuration of that tablet.

This is the iPad to go for as a potential laptop replacement capable of video editing and heavy graphics work. The OLED screen provides up to 1600 nits peak brightness for HDR work and a fast 120Hz refresh rate for zero lag.

The M4 iPad Air was only released in March of this year, so $100 off might be the best deal we see over Black Friday 2026, and it's not to be sniffed at. This is the iPad we recommend for most people as t's significantly more affordable than the pro, but still has Apple Pencil Pro support and enough power for digital drawing, photo editing and light video editing in Final Cut. There's also $100 off its larger 13-inch sibling.

The latest generation of the basic iPad is a good a choice as ever for anyone looking for a general, everyday tablet for browsing, entertainment and casual sketching and notetaking. This tablet was also released in March 2025, and Amazon had $70 off the original price during Black Friday last year, so this deal could (I would say should) get better.

A new iPad mini was released just this month with the faster A20 Pro chip. We've not seen any discounts on that yet, and its starting price is $100 more than that of its predecessor at $699. With a $130 difference when you consider this discount, the 2024 model is still worth considering. It's more powerful than the standard iPad and supports Apple Pencil Pro, making it a small but mighty option for sketching and notetaking on the go.

iPad Black Friday deals in the UK aren't great so far, but any saving is welcome on Apple's best tablet – we've not seen any discount at all since Apple hiked prices in April because of the RAM crisis.

Very has a small saving on the latest generation of the basic iPad, which we rated as a decent upgrade from its predecessor when we tested it earlier this year. This is one deal I would hope to see improved on as we get closer to Black Friday proper, but given high price of tech at the moment, who knows?

Compatible with the 2024 and 2025 iPad Pros and iPad Airs as well as the latest iPad mini, the Pencil Pro is Apple's most sophisticated iPad stylus, with haptic feedback, a pinch gesture to control actions and a barrel roll feature to change brushes. This fell as cheap as $89 during Black Friday last year, but 2025 prices feel like a long, long time ago today.

This is actually a really good deal on Apple's best inner-ear headphones yet. Released a year ago, they have improved Active Noise Cancellation and battery life compared to the previous gen AirPods Pro, as well as a better fit, improved water and dust resistance and a new heart rate sensor.

This the lowest price we've seen for a keyboard case that does two jobs in one, protecting your iPad (it's compatible with the latest 10in iPad) while also adding keyboard functionality, making the tablet convenient for work and email. We find Logitech's officially endorsed options are sleek and well built, and this is a very good saving.

Apple hiked the price of all of its current iPad models around the middle of 2026 because of the increase in the cost of components, particularly memory (RAM) and internal storage (SSDs). The whole consumer tech sector has been impacted by these price rises, which have been caused by a shortage of component due to the demand from companies building AI data centres.

This means that this year's iPad Black Friday deals will inevitably be more expensive than last year's. There's no sign that starting prices will fall again any time soon.

Keeping in mind the size of discounts seen during previous iPad Black Friday sales is a good way to gauge whether it's the right time to buy or if prices could fall further. The pattern we've seen is that the best deals on the latest generation of iPads tend to be up to $70 off the standard iPad and $100 off the iPad Air and up to $200 off higher-spec iPad Pros.

In 14 years of tracking prices, our experience is that there is rarely any difference between Black Friday and Cyber Monday iPad prices. They are usually the same deals under a different name. On a very few occasions, we have seen new discounts appear on Cyber Monday.

The best iPad for you will depend on what you want to use it for. For browsing, watching movies, social media and just occasional note taking and sketching, this year's standard 11-inch iPad with the A16 chip will do just fine, and it doesn't make sense to spend more. Aim to spend no more than $399 on this,

If you're an artist and want a more efficient drawing experience, I'd recommend stepping up to the iPad Air. A new M4-chipped generation of this tablet was released in March, and Amazon's already slashed the price by $100 in a Black Friday deal. This tablet comes in two choices of size: 11 inches or 13 inches.

If you're a professional artist and you have the budget for it, the iPad Pro is the top-of-the-range option. Also coming in 11- and 13-inch models, it has a superior screen with a bright OLED panel for improved contrast along along with a faster 120Hz refresh rate for a seamless drawing experience.

Coming with the M5 chip, this is the iPad to choose if you want to replace you're laptop when working on the go, and it's cut out to handle more demanding creative software, including video editing.

Remember that all iPads come in various configurations, with the option of WiFi and cellular connectivity or just WiFi alone, plus two size options for the Pro and Air and at least two choices of internal storage capacity. When quoting prices above, we've generally quoted the price of the base model with WiFi and the smallest SSD. This might not necessarily be the option that meets your needs, but retailers will usually list other configurations under the same product listing.

If you use a tablet for work and want to store large files on the device, you may need a higher capacity. The iPad Pro, for example, is available with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB or 2TB. the price rises notably, but the higher-spec models sometimes come in for bigger discounts.

We'll be linking directly to the best Black Friday iPad deals across all four models here on this page. The best thing you can do to prepare to choose the best deal for you is to think ahead about which iPad you want and in which configuration.

Once you've decided which iPad you want (the Pro, Air, mini or standard iPad), choose the size (there's a choice of 11in or 13in with the iPad Pro and iPad Air), whether you want cellular connectivity or WiFi alone and which storage capacity you'll think you need. Whether you can make do with the starting capacity or you need to hike it up to 512GB, or even 1TB or 2TB on the iPad Pro will depend on how you expect to use the device and whether you'll also be using cloud storage or will want to store large design or video files on the tablet itself.

Apple is unlikely to run any direct iPad Black Friday discounts itself. Instead, it's likely yo offer gift vouchers worth up to $100/£80 with the purchase of certain iPads. This might be appealing if you know that you're going to want to buy another Apple product in the future, but most people would be better off going for deals at third-party sites.

In previous years, we have seen good Black Friday iPad deals at most of the major retailers in the US and UK. In the US, Amazon and B&H Photo tend to have the best prices, while Walmart and Target can also be worth checking.

In the UK, Amazon and Very tend to have the biggest discounts, while Laptops Direct is worth checking for discounts on older models. We track prices at all of these retailers and more.

Traditionally, Black Friday was the Friday after Thanksgiving in the US. It's since extended to cover almost all of November at some retailers. As for when Black Friday ends, many retailers continue it until the Monday after Black Friday itself, which some call Cyber Monday. This year, that falls on 30 November 2026.

#9074. Yayoi Kusama sets $15m record as Sotheby’s opens New York mega-sales

Tom Eddison, Sotheby's co-head of contemporary art London, sells Yayoi Kusama's No. 3P.B. Courtesy Sotheby's

Just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a new auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees). The evening also saw records for Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts. Not a bad start to a week in which auction houses expect to sell as much as $2.4bn in art.

Kusama’s No. 3P.B. (1960) fetched $12.5m ($15m with fees), against an estimate of $10m to $15m, setting a new auction record for the Japanese artist who died in August. One of Kusama's earliest landmark Infinity Nets series, the painting was included in a 1961 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art, among the artist's earliest inclusions in an American institutional show. The work was the fifth most expensive lot in Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening auction, which brought in $224.78m ($268.7m with fees).

No. 3P.B. (1960) by Yayoi Kusuma. Courtesy Sotheby's

The 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale. While around 45% of lots hammered within their estimates, bidding was uneven.

Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) led the sale in terms of value, hammering for $22m ($24.6m with fees) against an estimate of $20m to $30m. It was followed by Willem de Kooning’s Water...Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975), which fell short of its $20m low estimate, hammering for $17.1m ($20.3m with fees). Andy Warhol’s Flowers (1964) fetched $15.2m ($18.2m with fees), just above its $15m high estimate.

Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $15m ($17.1m with fees), at the low end of its $15m to $20m estimate, setting a new auction record for the artist. It was a case of déjà vu: the same painting had previously set Francis’s auction record when it sold in 1999.

One of the most exciting moments of the evening came when five bidders battled for six minutes over Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991), a depiction of an Old English Sheepdog. The work ultimately hammered for $9m to a roar of applause.

Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991) Courtesy Sotheby's

Another standout result was Salman Toor’s Lavender Boy (2019), which went for $340,000 ($435,200 with fees), more than four times its $80,000 high estimate even without buyer's premium being factored in.

The evening kicked off with the single-owner sale of the collection of cable television magnate Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth. The 24-lot auction generated $90.8m ($109.9m with fees), comfortably within its $74.4m to $109m pre-sale estimate, with a 100% sell-through rate. However, one-third of the lots hammered below their low estimates, while just one-quarter exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1965-68), which hammered for $16.2m ($19.3m with fees), among the highest results for the artist at auction, against an estimate of $12m to $18m. The Baums acquired the work in 1986 for just $65,000; including Sotheby’s fees, the winning bidder paid almost 300 times that amount.

Roy Lichtenstein's Two Paintings Sleeping Muse (Study) (1983) Courtesy Sotheby's

It was followed by an untitled 1998 Mark Rothko painting, which fetched $15.5m ($17.7m with fees), surpassing its $10m to $15m estimate. The Baums purchased the work for $115,000 in 1983, according to Sotheby’s, meaning Monday’s buyer paid more than 150 times that amount, including fees. The third most valuable lot was Andy Warhol’s The Scream (After Munch) (1984), sold for $6.8m ($7.9m with fees) against an estimate of $4m to $6m. Together, the three works accounted for around 42% of the sale’s $91.4m hammer total.

Not every work met expectations. Franz Kline’s Figure (1955) recorded the largest shortfall in dollar terms, hammering for $1.8m ($2.3m with fees), against an estimate of $4m to $6m—55% below its low estimate.

After the sale, Sotheby’s said works from single-owner collections achieved $239m (with fees), making up almost 60% of the evening’s total earnings.

“When your sale is the opener for a major season like this, there’s always a sense of heightened anticipation," Lucius Elliott, Sotheby's head of contemporary art marquee sales, said following the auction. "I think this evening’s sale did what everyone hoped it would—signaled that the market is in a great place and demand is strong. We saw real competition for coveted works, with a keen focus both on works from admired collections and for the works we specifically sought out for this sale to meet the demand we knew was there. The evening’s final tally—double that of the equivalent evening last season—says it all.”

On Tuesday night, the New York art world's eyes will turn toward rival auction house Christie's for the 20th century auction, led by paintings with eight-figure estimates by Wassily Kandinsky, Gustav Klimt and Pablo Picasso.
