#9028. Sotheby’s Hospices de Beaune Charity Wine Sale Nets $15.8 M. in France, with One Barrel Selling for Record $1.1 M.

The annual Hospices de Beaune charity wine auction in Burgundy, France, organized by Sotheby’s, generated €14.4 million ($15.8 million) on Sunday. It was the 166th edition of the the historic sale, and its top lot—known as the “Presidents’ Barrel”—was bought by Brazilian wine merchant Aloar Pereira Linoa for €770,000 ($848,732) in the room.

Just after the hammer came down, there was a surprise twist; the Faiveley family, one of Bergundy’s most important wine-making dynasties, pledged another €230,000 ($251,000), rounding up the total to a cool €1 million ($1.1 million).The donation brought the charitable total to a new record. Proceeds from the 228-liter Presidents’ Barrel (exempt from Sotheby’s buyer’s premium fees), which holds a Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru, will go to ARSLA and DEBRA, two charities supporting people with rare diseases. They are charcot disease and epidermolysis bullosa, otherwise known as “butterfly skin disease.”Each year, celebrities are enlisted to rev up the crowd and encourage bidding on the main barrel. This year saw comedy duo Éric Judor and Ramzy Bedia, alongside actress Aurelie Vandevoorde, temporarily take over at the rostrum. At one point, Judor promised the next bidder a minor role in his new movie, as the French trio had the room in raptures during the 18-minute bidding battle. “All you New Yorkers here… you’re willing to pay $20 for a hotdog but you won’t pay for this wine?” he joked.I’ve never seen people singing at an auction before, but at one point the entire crowd erupted into a standing performance of “Ban Bourguignon,” Burgundy’s unofficial anthem. Everyone raised their hands to shoulder level and twisted their wrists back and forth in rhythm, singing: “La, la, la, la, la, la….,” on repeat. Related Articles At Sotheby's $378.7 M. Doubleheader, Buyers Take Risks Again, Even as Bidding Drags Yayoi Kusama 'Infinity Net' Painting Sells for $15.1 M. at Sotheby's, Setting a Record

There were more than 600 people in the Halles de Beanue, a thatched-roof market hall just across from the Hôtel-Dieu de Beaune in the center of town. More than 350 registered participants from over 30 countries took part in the sale, with collectors also tuning in from a viewing event at Marcel in New York.“Like a work of art, every great Burgundy wine tells a story of place, time, and craftmanship,” Celian Ravel d’Estiennen Sotheby’s head of auction sales for wine in France, told ARTnews. “The 166th Hospices de Beaune sale celebrated precisely this heritage, as well as the generosity that has defined the event since 1859. The €1 million raised for the charities was a powerful testament to the emotional and cultural value of wine.”The Hospices de Beaune’s chief winemaker, Ludavine Griveau, was in tears as Vandevoorde brought the gavel down. “We can all be very proud of the work accomplished,” she said.This year’s sale featured wines from the 2026 vintage, which was shaped by prolonged heat and dry conditions, including 53 days of heatwave. Harvesting began on August 15 in Pouilly-Fuissé, Beaune, and Meursault, the earliest start in the history of the Domaine des Hospices de Beaune, and wrapped up on August 24 in the Côte de Nuits. Yields were low, putting Griveau and her team under extra pressure, but the resulting wines were praised for their quality.In total, 48 barrels of 34 red wines and 86 barrels, including two half-barrels, of 18 white wines were sold, alongside 12 barrels and three half-barrels of eaux-de-vie. The auction ran over five hours. The average hammer price for a barrel of red and white wine was €31,156, marking the sixth consecutive year in which the figure has topped €30,000. Reds performed particularly well, with their average price rising 5 percent on last year to €28,931. White wines, meanwhile, saw something of a correction, according to Guillaume Koch, director and chairman of the board of the Hospices Civils de Beaune.

“The overall result of the sale is in line with our expectations, given the volumes offered this year,” Koch said. “We have seen the outstanding quality of the red wines duly recognised, while prices for the great white wines have undergone a correction.”Among the standout results were a barrel of Mazis-Chambertin Grand Cru, Cuvée Madeleine Collignon, which sold for €185,000, a record for the appellation; a barrel of Meursault Premier Cru Les Genevrières, Cuvée Philippe Le Bon, at €75,000; and a barrel of Pommard Premier Cru Les Epenots, Cuvée Dom Gobelet, at €40,000. Four of the five Pommard Village and Premier Cru cuvées offered also achieved new auction records.

Every November, the auction raises money for the Hospices Civils de Beaune, a charitable hospital network founded in the 15th century to care for the sick and poor. Proceeds from this year’s sale will also go towards a major program of digital modernisation, including a new electronic patient record system and investment in laboratory and medical imaging equipment.The Hospices de Beaune auction took place alongside the town’s annual Trois Glorieuses, a three-day celebration of Burgundy’s wine and gastronomic heritage. The festivities brought together winemakers, négociants, collectors, and wine lovers for tastings, special dinners, and celebrations across Beaune and the surrounding vineyards, transforming the town into the center of the Burgundian wine world for the weekend. It’s pretty boozy, and lots of fun.Sotheby’s has been making a broader push into the global wine market, expanding its international reach through new specialist appointments, high-profile sales, and events designed to attract a younger generation of collectors. Its wine auction sales reached $127.5 million in 2025, up 12 percent year-on-year, with Burgundy accounting for 39 percent of the total.

The house has held the Hospices de Beaune auction contract since 2021 and it runs until 2030. The house took it over from Christie’s, which ran it from 2005 to 2021.

#9026. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

This week on Dezeen, Japanese electronics company Sony launched a remake of its original Walkman headphones, which have colourful foam pads and lean into 1980s nostalgia.

The headphones, called MDR-3R, resemble the model that debuted with the first portable Walkman cassette player in 1979. However, the new edition has a USB-C connector that works with most modern devices.

Other design news included Swedish designer Gustaf Westman’s unveiling of his full collection for media company Disney, including a bookstand shaped like Donald Duck and a mirror that resembles Pluto.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” Westman told Dezeen about working with the familiar characters.

American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny informed by a compliment architect Álvaro Siza once gave him, telling Holl he used colour “like Matisse”.

The colourful watch, which has a three-dimensional dial with red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks, was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects.

A housing development in Andorra designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos has been damaged in a fire.

Access to the spiral staircase, which leads up to the roof and has become a popular spot for photos, now costs £5.60 per person. Snøhetta told Dezeen that “visitor management is necessary”.

As rumours about the casting of the next James Bond began to hot up this week, my phone has been busy. Most of my friends (hello, both!) know me as a huge James Bond fan, and have wanted to know who I thought was going to get the role. Well, one thing's for sure, I told them all. It won't be Pattinson. Mark my words. He's just too famous.

So you can imagine my surprise when Robert Pattinson was indeed announced as the new James Bond this afternoon. Everything about the news feels bizarre to me, including the lack of press release and associated fanfare (whereas Daniel Craig rode down the Thames on a speedboat, Pattinson was announced via a simple social media post). But the biggest shock is that Pattinson is by far the most famous person to be cast in the role. He's the first bonafide A-lister to pick up the Walther PPK. He's Batman, for God's sake. For better or worse, the Bond brand changed forever today. And it's thanks to one name: Amazon.

It perhaps isn't surprising that Blofeld's—sorry, Bezos's—company has opted for such a bankable star. The company paid billions to acquire MGM (which owned the rights to Bond), and will want a return on its investment. But the whole thing seems so at odds with the ethos of the previous Bond custodians. "I felt I had to have an unknown actor, not a star," producer Cubby Broccoli said of the search for the very first Bond. "Above all, a man you’d believe could be James Bond."

For decades, Bond has been one of the most carefully controlled brands in entertainment. The gun barrel sequence, the theme tune, the 007 logo, the Aston Martin; every element is instantly recognisable, and has been meticulously protected by the Broccoli family. Bond films have always felt like events, partly because they don't come along very often. But Amazon doesn't do scarcity, it does content. And with the company now in creative control of the franchise, it's hard not to wonder how long it will be before 007 becomes less of a cinematic institution and more of an endlessly expandable IP. I'm not sure I'm ready for the 'Young Q' spin-off.

There are, of course, opportunities here. Bond has arguably been in need of a shake-up for some time, and Pattinson is a genuinely exciting actor, capable of bringing something strange, unpredictable and perhaps even uncomfortable to a character that has occasionally felt trapped by his own iconography. But the choice also feels like a statement of intent from Amazon. Where previous Bond actors were largely blank canvases onto which the 007 identity could be projected, Pattinson arrives with a huge, established brand of his own. Rather than making a star out of Bond, Amazon has bought a star to sell Bond. It's a subtle distinction, but a significant one. Am I going to be able to look up at the screen and see James Bond, rather than Robert Pattinson in a suit?

But while it'll be Pattinson's name that hogs the headlines, the bigger question isn't simply what kind of Bond Pattinson will be, but what kind of brand Amazon wants Bond to become. Will the company recognise that Bond's enduring appeal lies partly in his exclusivity, his mystique, and his ability to remain just a little out of reach? For all of his reinventions, 007 has always felt bigger than the actor playing him. Until today.

#9022. Who Sat for Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait? A New Catalog Essay Suggests It May Have Been the Artist

The catalog for the exhibition “Van Eyck: The Portraits” opening at London’s National Gallery on November 21, has reignited a long-standing debate about the identity of couple in the Early Netherlandish master’s mysterious Arnolfini Portrait (1434). As reported in the Art Newspaper, one of the catalog’s essays suggests that the man in the painting, usually identified as a member of the Arnolfini family of Italian merchants, is in fact Jan van Eyck himself.

In the painting, which is owned by the National Gallery and a centerpiece of the show, an elegantly dressed man and woman pose hand in hand in a private room. Every item in the chamber, including the couple’s fur-trimmed clothing, the oriental carpet on the floor, and even the orange resting on a windowsill—an expensive luxury at the time—signals understated wealth. Related Articles Clark Art Institute Unveils its Massive Aso Tavitian Gift, To Be Housed in a Brand-New Wing: 'Any Curator or Director's Dream' Why Is Hieronymus Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights So Important?

The man and the woman are clearly husband and wife, though the work does not, as was once believed, depict a marriage ceremony. A 16th-century inventory of the holdings of Margaret of Austria, the painting’s owner at the time, identifies it as “Hernoul le Fin” or “Arnoult Fin,” which is widely interpreted by art historians as “Arnolfini.”

Scholars have disagreed however, however, about which Arnolfini the man in the painting might be. Possible candidates are either Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (though recent discoveries suggest he was not married at the time the painting was made), or more likely his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, who would have been in his late thirties in 1434.

Giovanni’s first wife Costanza Trenta died in 1433; thus, according to the National Gallery’s website, the woman is probably his second wife, whose identity is unknown. Alternatively, as art historian Margaret Koster and others have suggested, the painting may be a memorial piece.

It is also possible that the sitters were friends of Van Eyck’s. Reflected in the convex mirror behind them, two more men can be seen entering the room. Prominently written on the wall above the mirror is the inscription “Johannes de Eyck fuit hic. 1434” (“Jan van Eyck was here. 1434”), which is sometimes taken to mean that the men in the mirror are Van Eyck and his servant arriving for a visit.

But Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in one of the catalog’s essays, asserts instead that the subjects of the painting are Van Eyck and his wife Margaret. Kemperdick is a curator at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which owns several Van Eycks, including Portrait of a Man in a Red Chaperon (1390–1440/41) of the same man in the Arnolfini Portrait at an older age. He bases his theory on the inscription’s placement in the Arnolfini Portrait next to the male figure’s head, arguing that this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man.

If true, Kemperdick’s theory would throw the identification of the subjects in other Van Eyck paintings into doubt. The National Gallery’s Portrait of a Man (1433), of a much older man than the man in the Arnolfini Portrait, is currently tentatively identified as a self-portrait, while the entry for the Berlin work—Kemperdick’s theory notwithstanding—still notes that it is presumed to be of Giovanni Arnolfini. (Both Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) and Portrait of a Man in a Red Chaperon (Giovanni Arnolfini?) are included in the exhibition, which brings together all nine of Van Eyck’s surviving portraits.)

For his part, Nicholas Flory, the exhibition’s co-curator along with Emma Capron, told the Art Newspaper that he found Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative.” He notes that the sitter in another work in the show from the Musea Brugge, definitively known to be of Margaret based on an inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.

German art historian Till-Holger Borchert, the former director of the Musea Brugge—concurs, finding the 16th-century inventory reference near conclusive proof that the painting is of an Arnolfini. But, he added, given how little is known about Van Eyck’s life, “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”

#9021. Mexico's Parque del Jaguar protects jaguars with 18-kilometre limestone wall

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 has created an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest at Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

Rather than creating a conventional enclosed nature reserve, Colectivo C733 designed a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals‘ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The park occupies a coastal territory containing tropical forest, mangroves, underground rivers and karstic geology, as well as the ancient Mayan archaeological site of Tulum.

Its landscape had also been affected by contaminated soil around a former airstrip and habitat disruption caused by the Cancún-Tulum highway.

At its perimeter, the studio added an 18-kilometre dry-stacked limestone wall, known locally as a tecorral, informed by traditional Mayan stone boundaries.

Built without mortar, the wall allows wildlife to move through gaps between the stones while establishing a physical boundary around the protected area.

Within the park, Colectivo C733 introduced a number of public buildings and viewing platforms, concentrating new construction in previously altered areas and leaving large sections of the territory untouched.

Low-impact transport routes, including pedestrian and cycling paths, connect the different areas, with electric transport also introduced to reduce the impact of visitor movement.

The routes link the park’s public facilities with its archaeological and ecological sites.

At the central entrance, a timber-framed building is screened by closely spaced vertical wooden members and topped with a woven palm-thatch roof.

The complex accommodates a museum, cafe, shop, multipurpose room and open-air forum, alongside a kitchen designed for cooking over smoke.

Other structures include elevated observation towers and a long suspended walkway that crosses the forest canopy, revealing different aspects of the area’s geology, water systems and biodiversity as visitors move through it.

“By designing how the territory is revealed, inhabited, and understood over time, Parque del Jaguar shifts architecture from a static intervention to an evolving framework that connects environment, culture, and collective awareness,” Colectivo C733 said.

Access is more controlled in sensitive areas, helping to limit disturbance to wildlife habitats, including those used by jaguars.

At the coast, stone platforms, stepped seating and raised timber staircases provide access to viewpoints overlooking the Caribbean Sea.

The buildings use locally sourced limestone, chicozapote timber, sascab – a naturally occurring limestone-based material – and palm thatch.

Green roofs, shaded outdoor spaces and naturally ventilated structures help reduce the need for mechanical cooling in the tropical climate.

Alongside the construction work, the project includes soil remediation, reforestation and the recovery of natural water systems.

Asphalt has been removed from previously developed areas as part of efforts to restore the ground and reconnect habitats.

Founded in 2019, Colectivo C733 brings together the practices of Gabriela Carrillo, Carlos Facio, José Amozurrutia, Eric Valdez and Israel Espín to work on public architecture and urban infrastructure across Mexico.

Its other projects featured on Dezeen include a square-shaped pedestrian pier that hovers over a lagoon in Bacalar, Mexico and a brick music school topped with a cantilevered coconut wood roof in Nacajuca, Mexico.

#9020. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

#9018. Yayoi Kusama ‘Infinity Net’ Painting Sells for $15.1 M. at Sotheby’s, Setting a Record

Just months after Yayoi Kusama‘s death, one of her paintings sold at Sotheby’s New York on Monday night for a hammer price of $12.5 million, or $15.1 million with fees, setting a new auction record for the artist.

The work sold after a brief bidding war between Evelyn Lin, chairman of modern and contemporary art, Asia, and Lisa Dennison, chairman of the Americas, both of whom were bidding on behalf of clients on the phone. Lin ultimately prevailed after 10 bids over the course of four minutes. The $12.5 million hammer price placed the work squarely within its presale estimate of $10 million to $15 million. Related Articles Sotheby's Hospices de Beaune Charity Wine Sale Nets $15.8 M. in France, with One Barrel Selling for Record $1.1 M. Sotheby's $180 M. Van Gogh Sale Faces Eleventh-Hour Nazi-Era Restitution Claim

No. 3P.B. (1960), is one of Kusama’s “Infinity Net” paintings, a series of large-scale monochrome abstractions in which the canvas is covered with thousands of looping brushstrokes. Kusama painted her first “Infinity Net” work in 1958, shortly after moving from Japan to New York, which makes No. 3P.B. a rare early example of the form. The crimson canvas, which stands more than five feet tall, appeared in the Whitney Museum’s 1961 painting-focused annual exhibition, a precursor to the Whitney Biennial.

About 10 lots later on Monday night, another painting from the series, Infinity Nets (OZEH), sold for a hammer price of $2.5 million, or $3.06 million with fees. That work, a white canvas measuring roughly 6½ by 8½ feet, is far more recent, dating to 2011.

Like Kusama’s “Infinity Mirror Rooms,” which are more popular on social media, the “Infinity Net” series deals with obsession and repetition. The series is often said to prefigure the Minimalism and Post-Minimalism of the 1960s and 1970s, and it made her name in a male-dominated art world. Reviewing the paintings for ARTnews in 1959, Donald Judd wrote, “The expression transcends the question of whether it is Oriental or American. Although it is something of both, certainly of such Americans as Rothko, Still and Newman, it is not at all a synthesis and is thoroughly independent.”

Since Kusama died in August at 97, nearly 30 of her works have come to auction at Sotheby’s, Christie’s, and Phillips. The top results have been for two paintings of pumpkins, another of her signature motifs. At Sotheby’s Hong Kong in September, the 2010 painting Pumpkin (TWPOT) sold for HK$60.7 million, or about $7.74 million. The next day at Christie’s Hong Kong, the 2011 painting A-Pumpkin (YHP), which shows a yellow pumpkin on a patterned black background, sold for HK$58.2 million, or about $7.43 million.

Besides No. 3P.B., 11 more Kusama works will go on the block this week. Five of them are “Infinity Net” paintings, but none is nearly as early or as highly valued.

Kusama’s previous auction record was set in 2022 at Phillips New York by the 1959 painting Untitled (Nets), 1959, a white “Infinity Net” made a year before No. 3P.B. It sold for $10.5 million with fees.

#9017. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#9015. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#9014. Japanese sauna by Daichi Inc makes "people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest"

Tree trunks puncture the slim timber platforms of this minimalist sauna in a Japanese woodland, designed by local architecture studio Daichi Inc.

Named Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna, the project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

According to Daichi Inc, the idea for the project was to make the trees feel “part of the architecture itself”, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

The sauna has been shortlisted in the Leisure and wellness category of Dezeen Awards 2026.

“Conventional architecture typically clears nature away, cutting down thick and strong trees and transforming them into standardised building materials,” said the studio.

“In this project, however, the existing trees were preserved and used directly as part of the spatial framework, blurring the boundary between nature and the built environment,” it added.

“Rather than placing architecture on top of nature, the project allows architecture to coexist with it, creating an immersive bodily experience in which people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest itself.”

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna’s structure comprises two stacked timber decks and a roof, with the central platform partially supported by the site’s natural slope.

The thin planes sit atop timber grids supported by the trees themselves and punctured by small circular cut-outs through which their trunks can grow.

Timber steps connect these different platforms, culminating on the upper level where the central sauna room sits, wrapped in frameless glass panels. It contains a wooden bench and a central log burner.

Aside from the sauna room and a small plunge pool, the decks are left entirely open and flexible, and are surrounded by slender metal balustrades at their edges.

“Wood and glass were used as the primary materials, while the existing trees themselves were integrated into the architectural framework,” said the studio.

“Decks and sauna spaces were carefully positioned to appear as if floating within the forest,” it added. “The forest is not treated as a backdrop, but functions as an essential structural part of the architecture itself

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include Puusauna in Finland by architect Jaakko Torvinen, which is supported by whole, charred tree trunks sourced from the neighbouring forest, and an off-grid bathhouse in London.

#9013. At Sotheby’s $378.7 M. Doubleheader, Buyers Take Risks Again, Even as Bidding Drags

By Daniel Cassady, Harrison Jacobs November 17, 2026 12:44am

Sotheby’s kicked off the November marquee sales with a doubleheader on Monday evening that generated $378.7 million across 74 lots. The top-line results look solid, but a sluggish second half seemed to further illustrate the choosy mood among collectors right now.

The nearly three-hour marathon started strong with the dedicated sale from the collection of cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum. It was a white-glove result, with all 24 works sold for a hammer total of $90.9 million. With fees, the sale landed at $110 million, just a shade above the presale high estimate of $109 million. Related Articles Yayoi Kusama 'Infinity Net' Painting Sells for $15.1 M. at Sotheby's, Setting a Record Sotheby's Hospices de Beaune Charity Wine Sale Nets $15.8 M. in France, with One Barrel Selling for Record $1.1 M.

The Baum sale was a lively affair from the start. After the first lot—Roy Lichtenstein’s 1983 cut-paper work Two Paintings: Sleeping Muse (Study)—sparked a four-minute contest among three specialists and a bidder in the room, CEO Charles Stewart strode over to Gareth Jones, the house’s chief marketing officer, and said of the $3.8 million total, “Well, that’s a good start.” Three lots later, a Lucio Fontana copper canvas with a glorious cut down the middle ignited another bidding war, the bids ricocheting among three bidders in the room. It hammered at $3.5 million, or $4.4 million with fees, well above the $3 million high estimate.

Oliver Barker, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, handled the proceedings with panache, making even a fairly ordinary stretch of bidding feel brisk. Amid the bidding for Lot 7, Andy Warhol’s 1984 painting The Scream (After Munch), he teased Jacqueline Wachter, chairwoman of private sales, for taking a bit too long with her phone bidder, asking whether she was “doing her shopping or doing her conversions.” Then he quipped to the audience, “Amazon is always open. As is Sotheby’s Dot Com.” It was a little sharp, perhaps, but it got a laugh and helped lighten the mood as the sale began to drag.

The crowded salesroom was a who’s who of the art trade: Dominique Lévy, Brett Gorvy, Amalia Dayan, David Schrader, Emmanuel Di Donna, Christophe Van de Weghe, and Gagosian Art Advisory’s Bernard Lagrange were just a few of the heavies in attendance.

In the end, six works hammered above their estimates and another 10 landed in range, with spirited bidding throughout, both in the room and on the phone. Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest led the sale at $19.3 million, followed by Mark Rothko’s Untitled at $17.7 million and Ed Ruscha’s Dimple at $11.6 million. The Baums had bought the Mitchell privately in 1986 for just $65,000, making its sale price nearly 300 times what they paid. The Rothko, which they acquired for $115,000 in 1983, brought more than 150 times its purchase price. Not bad for a few decades of collecting. The final lot in the sale, Mario Merz’s neon sculpture Iguana, sold well below its estimate, but that did little to dampen the enthusiasm, as the room erupted in applause.

The Now and Contemporary sale that followed was considerably less celebratory. Of the 53 lots originally offered, three were withdrawn before the sale, and another five went unsold: works by Kerry James Marshall, Ellsworth Kelly, Roy Lichtenstein, and Keith Haring, and, curiously, a Formula One race car. Tom Eddison, head of contemporary art at Sotheby’s London, who took over auctioneering duties for the sale, said the car was a first for the auction house, and it required a lengthy preamble explaining that the sale was subject to the terms of service of RM Sotheby’s, the house’s classic-car affiliate. The car garnered a handful of bids but failed to reach its low estimate before Eddison declared it unsold. It may be some time before Sotheby’s tries that experiment again.

That’s not to say the results for the contemporary sale were lackluster. When all was said and done, the sale garnered a hammer total of $224.8 million. With fees, the total climbed to $268.8 million, within the presale aggregate estimate of $226.2 million to $323 million, and well above the equivalent sale in November 2025, which generated $178.5 million. Of course, we should note that last year’s sale followed the trove of works from the late cosmetics heir Leonard Lauder, which generated an eye-watering $527.5 million. Alas, not every season sees three Klimts hit the block.

Of the 45 lots that sold, a full 14 hammered above their presale estimates, and another 24 landed in range. Still, while there always seemed to be a handful of bidders for each sold lot, with Eddison darting his hands left, right, and center, most works hammered after only a minute or two.

The most protracted bidding wars came somewhat early. A six-minute contest among four specialists for Jeff Koons’s 1991 sculpture Bob-Tail ended with contemporary art specialist Bame Fierro March winning the lot for a hammer price of $9 million. At $10.7 million with fees, that’s good for just over three times the high estimate. (Is Koons’s market trending back up, or do collectors just really like an adorable English sheepdog?) Seven lots later, Agnes Martin’s cream canvas Desert, from the collection of Lenore and Bernard Greenberg, sold after a six-minute duel between contemporary art specialist Alya Sama and Lisa Dennison, chairman of the Americas. Dennison won on a $9.2 million hammer bid, or $11.3 million with fees, comfortably above the $8 million high estimate. And Andy Warhol’s 1964–65 painting Flowers fetched $18.2 million with fees against a $10 million to $15 million estimate.

Mark the Warhol and Koons results as green shoots for a market that’s spent much of the past two years playing it safe. Neither artist has had the easiest time in the secondary market lately, which makes those results particularly interesting. Something to watch going forward, especially for Koons.

After the sale, Dennison pointed to the continued strength of early Martin paintings, which have been outperforming expectations for several seasons.

Art adviser Ed Dolman similarly found the night’s results encouraging. In a text message toward the end of the sale, he said, “The best works always do fine, [but] buyers were taking some risks again.”

Dolman also pointed to the depth of bidding. While 29 of the 45 sold lots in the contemporary sale had guarantees—as did every work in the Baum sale—those guarantors were often outbid on Monday night. Buyers, it seemed, were willing to go a little further.

Not that everything was suddenly flying off the walls. Lichtenstein’s Reflections on ‘Painter and Model,’ the top lot of the contemporary sale at $24.7 million with fees, came in well short of the high end of its $20 million to $30 million estimate. Willem de Kooning’s Water…Soft Banks of a Window (Untitled VIII) brought $20.3 million, just above its $20 million low estimate, while Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I made $17.1 million against a $15 million to $20 million estimate.

The buzziest result of the night was no doubt for Yayoi Kusama’s 1960 painting No. 3P.B., which hammered for $12.5 million after 10 bids spread across four minutes. With fees, the result came to $15.1 million, just above the $15 million high estimate, and good for a new record for the artist, who died in August. About 10 lots later, another of her “Infinity Nets” paintings, Infinity Nets (OZEH), sold for a hammer price of $2.5 million, or $3.1 million with fees, just a shade above the $3 million high estimate. That work, a white canvas measuring roughly 6½ by 8½ feet, is far more recent, dating to 2011. And if you missed out on those two Kusamas, have no fear: Another 10 works of hers will hit the block over the rest of marquee week. Five are from her long-running “Infinity Nets” series.

Yet, for all the strong prices, the second half of the contemporary sale was a slog. With Eddison at the rostrum, the pace slowed considerably. Bids were drawn out, pauses stretched on, and even works that eventually fetched impressive prices seemed to take an age to get there. A few market watchers wondered whether such a sluggish tempo might discourage bidders, particularly on works that didn’t have much competition to begin with. It was an odd contrast: a sale that sometimes felt as though it was struggling to find its rhythm, even as buyers were spending millions more than expected.

To Nina Del Rio, an art adviser and auction house veteran, the results looked remarkably strong, particularly given the subdued energy in the second half of the sale. Still, she said, there hasn’t been much evidence of a shift in the market. At least not a fundamental one. Buyers appear to be behaving much as they did in May, when the best works attracted serious money but enthusiasm for younger artists remained muted. A few years ago, the Now sale was where collectors went to get their hands on artists whose waiting lists seemed impossible to crack. That sense of urgency has largely disappeared.

What collectors do seem willing to pay for is scarcity. Del Rio pointed to the modern masterpieces coming up later in the week, the sort of works that rarely appear at auction and may not come around again for decades. Among them is Wednesday’s sale of the Blaquier Collection, a group of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterpieces said to be worth around $450 million, and a $180 million Van Gogh suddenly subject to a last-minute restitution claim.

Dennison warned against reading too much into a single evening. Given the current mood, starting the week with contemporary art rather than a mix of modern and contemporary masterpieces makes it harder to judge the market as a whole. And while works in the $10 million to $20 million range performed well, the sale lacked the $30 million, $40 million, and $50 million trophies that drive enthusiasm across the whole week.

As for that Formula One car, Dennison said the result left her scratching her head. The last bid offered, $3.9 million, was just under the $4 million low estimate. Did the interested buyer really think the $100,000 gap was too wide to bridge?

There is a risk to putting something unexpected into a contemporary art sale. But, as Dennison pointed out, sometimes it works, as when Christie’s sold the Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton “Stan” during its 20th Century Evening Sale in 2020 for $31.8 million, nearly quadruple the high estimate.

Sotheby’s shouldn’t give up on the idea. There’s something appealing about an evening sale that doesn’t draw a firm boundary around paintings and sculptures. Not every experiment works the first time, or even the second. And if the object is truly one-of-a-kind, buyers are ready to shell out the cash.

#9012. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

Prince George made the headlines recently by displaying his artistic flair. The second in line to the throne impressed readers of Country Life magazine last week, when his colour pencil drawing of a kingfisher appeared in a special issue guest edited by his father, the Prince of Wales.

Shortly afterwards, the drawing went viral and amazed audiences on social media as well. It’s not hard to see why. The bird, which is playfully perched on a little branch and looking away from the viewer, demonstrates a level of craft you might not expect to come from the hands of a 12-year-old.

If you wish you could draw this well, and you’ve exhausted all of our how to draw tutorials, you might be in luck. Because shrewd online detectives may have figured out the secret behind the Prince’s handiwork.

Upon being shared on the likes of X and Instagram, people couldn’t believe how good the drawing was. Some commenters pointed out that he may have inherited his artistic talent from his family. After all, Prince George’s grandfather, King Charles, is an avid watercolour painter, and his parents both studied art at A-level. Catherine even studied history of art while at university.

The internet being what it is though, it wasn’t long until jealous users credited the drawing’s success to the amount of time and extra tuition the Prince surely enjoyed. However it seems he may have simply followed an easily accessible online course.

In amongst the comments, it soon became apparent that Prince George’s drawing bears more than a passing resemblance to the kingfisher featured in Matt Fussell’s course titled 3 Little Birds. And while no official confirmation has been made at the time of writing, everything from the pose to the positioning on the branch appears to be very similar.

This isn’t to take away from the Prince’s drawing. His picture still showcases a great level of skill and a keen understanding of the materials. In this case, if he followed the tutorial to the letter, Prince George used wax-based Prismacolor Premier Pencils on smooth Bristol paper. Both of which can be easily picked up from most local art supply shops.

#9010. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

#9009. Artsy and Artnet Acquire First Thursday as Art-Tech Expansion Picks Up Speed

Artsy and Artnet have another deal: The two art-market platforms announced the acquisition of First Thursday, a London-based startup that uses artificial intelligence to help galleries keep track of collectors, manage relationships, and, ideally, sell more art.

The purchase comes seven months after Artsy and Artnet joined forces under Beowolff Capital, the investment firm founded by Andrew Wolff. And just last week, Artnet announced a partnership with Kalshi, the prediction-market platform that allows users to bet on auction results, prompting a rather unenthusiastic response from parts of the art world. Related Articles Investor Says Artnet Layoffs Were Necessary for 'Financial Strength' Artnet Makes Significant Layoffs Following Consolidation with Artsy

The latest deal, whose financial terms weren’t disclosed, is a little less controversial. It also gives a clearer picture of what the combined company is trying to build: a single system that galleries can use to manage almost every part of their businesses.

Founded in 2023 by Callum Hale-Thomson, First Thursday specializes in what it calls “collector intelligence.” In practice, that means gathering years of emails, sales records, inquiries, and notes into one searchable place, then using AI to help dealers figure out which collectors might be interested in a particular work.

Hale-Thomson, whose parents are both artists, told ARTnews that the idea came to him after he spent six months working inside London galleries, effectively serving as their IT guy and watching how they operated. He found that many were sitting on years of valuable information without an easy way to use it.

“You’re sitting on an unbelievable trove of information,” he said, describing the emails, notebooks, and other records galleries accumulate over time. The problem was finding anything useful when it was needed.

First Thursday’s existing software helps with that. At an art fair, for example, a dealer can scan a visitor’s business card, record which painting caught their eye, and send a follow-up email directly from thier phone. The system can also bring together past correspondence and publicly available information about collectors, helping galleries identify potential buyers they might otherwise have overlooked.

Under the new ownership, Hale-Thomson and his team will help develop a broader gallery-management platform, scheduled to launch for select Artsy and Artnet partners in early 2027. It will combine collector records with inventory management, sales tools, invoicing, marketing, and online viewing rooms. Galleries will also be able to publish works to Artsy and Artnet directly from the system.

The initial focus will be smaller galleries, which often lack the money or staff to maintain sophisticated software.

Alex Forbes, who oversees global partnerships for Artsy and Artnet, told ARTnews that the smallest gallery partners will be able to use the core system without paying more than they already do for their Artsy subscriptions.

Larger galleries will be able to purchase additional features and access for bigger teams. Exact pricing will be announced when the platform launches.

“We want it to be the easiest to start out with for a small gallery,” Forbes said, while also making it useful for businesses with more complicated operations.

The move takes Artsy and Artnet further into a competitive market for gallery software, where established companies such as Artlogic already offer inventory and business-management tools. Last year, Artlogic merged with ArtCloud, another sign of consolidation in the art-tech business. (Artsy is already integrated with Artlogic and Artcloud, which, according to an Artsy spokesperson, the company will continue to support.)

Forbes acknowledged that galleries have different needs and that no single product will necessarily suit everyone. But he said the broader plan is to connect the company’s existing marketplaces and pricing data with the software that galleries use to run their businesses.

One potentially sensitive question is what happens to all that collector information. Artsy and Artnet say galleries will retain control of their data, which will remain private unless they choose to share it with the platforms.

For Hale-Thomson, who will remain with the business, the opportunity is to bring more sophisticated tools to galleries that haven’t traditionally been able to afford them.

And for Artsy and Artnet, the acquisition marks another step toward becoming something considerably bigger than two websites where people look at art, check prices, and occasionally buy something. Increasingly, they want to provide the software that keeps the business running.

That's the Category 1 Hyatt sweet spot — and it's the single most accessible, repeatable, high-value redemption in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A standard night at a Hyatt Place or Hyatt House in a mid-size U.S. city routinely runs **$100–$200 per night** in cash. At 5,000 points per night, you're redeeming at **2–4 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that demolishes the standard 1 cent per point benchmark that most casual rewards users never surpass. At 4 CPP on a $200 night, you're getting four times the value of a simple cash-back card. Every. Single. Time. The pricing inefficiency here is structural, not accidental. World of Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** — meaning a Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in January or a Friday night during a sold-out college football weekend when cash rates are spiking. The loyalty program doesn't dynamically price awards the way airlines do. That fixed ceiling is your edge. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption isn't just good — it's foundational. It's the first sweet spot that proves the system works. Before you're ready to redeem 60,000 points for a business class flight to Tokyo, you need to feel what it's like to hand over a handful of points and walk into a hotel room that would have cost you real money. This is that moment. It builds the muscle memory, the confidence, and the conviction that travel rewards are real — and that you're playing the game correctly. This is where the journey starts.

World of Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value of any major hotel loyalty program. While Hilton and Marriott have moved to dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate based on demand — Hyatt maintains a fixed award chart. This structural difference is your edge. A Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it is a quiet Tuesday in February or a sold-out homecoming weekend. Combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer ratios (1:1 from Sapphire Reserve, 4:3 from Sapphire Preferred) and instant transfer speed, Hyatt redemptions are the single best use of UR points for hotel stays. The ChooseFI community considers this the entry point that proves the entire travel rewards system works.

The core insight behind this sweet spot is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt uses a fixed-price award chart, and Category 1 is priced at a floor that hasn't kept pace with rising hotel cash rates.

Most hotel loyalty programs have moved to dynamic pricing — meaning award nights fluctuate with demand, just like cash rates. Marriott Bonvoy, Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards — they've all largely eliminated fixed charts in favor of algorithms that squeeze more points out of you when demand is high. Hyatt has held the line on a fixed chart, and that stubbornness is your opportunity.

The Category 1 floor sits at 5,000 points per night. As cash rates for qualifying properties have climbed with inflation — many now regularly pricing at $150–$200+ — the points cost has remained anchored. The gap between what the market charges and what Hyatt charges in points is widening in your favor every year. That's not a bug in the system. It's a feature you're uniquely positioned to exploit by understanding it.

This redemption is built on two of the best transferable points currencies available to everyday consumers:

Both transfers are instant, which means you can search for availability before committing your points, confirm the room you want is bookable, and then initiate the transfer and complete the booking — all in one sitting. This is a critical distinction from some airline partners where transfers take 24–72 hours and you're transferring on faith. With Hyatt, there's no leap of faith required.

The transfer ratio matters. With a Sapphire Reserve, every UR point becomes one Hyatt point — 15,000 UR points covers three Category 1 nights with zero waste. With a Sapphire Preferred, the 4:3 ratio means you need 20,000 UR points for the same 15,000 Hyatt points. Bilt transfers at 1:1.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award bookings. This matters more for higher-tier redemptions, but it's worth internalizing as a feature of the program overall. When you book 5,000 points for a hotel night, that's your cost. You'll pay any applicable taxes at checkout — typically $10–$25 — but there are no program-imposed carrier fees or redemption surcharges eating into your value.

Hyatt's full chart runs from 3,500 points (Category 1 standard) up to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. Understanding this structure helps you see the Category 1 sweet spot in context: it's the entry point, but it's not a consolation prize. Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties are upper-midscale hotels — clean, well-maintained, often with free breakfast at Hyatt House locations and complimentary parking in suburban markets. These aren't budget motels. You're getting a genuinely comfortable night's sleep for points that most people have already earned without trying.

Booking a Category 1 Hyatt award is one of the smoothest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's exactly how to do it from start to finish.

Before anything else, log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards or your Bilt Rewards account at biltrewards.com and confirm your current points balance. You need a minimum of 5,000 points per night to execute this redemption. If you have 15,000 points, you can book up to three nights.

Go to hyatt.com and log in or create a free World of Hyatt account (it's free to join). Use the search bar to enter your destination city and travel dates. Once results populate, filter by "Points" or "Use Points" using the toggle at the top of the results page. This will display the award rate alongside the cash rate for every property.

Filter further by selecting "Category 1–2" under the Points filter to quickly surface the lowest-cost options. Availability is typically strong — Hyatt.com shows real-time award inventory, and Category 1 properties almost always have rooms open. The booking window extends 395 days out, so you can plan well in advance for travel around a specific event.

Once you've found the property and dates you want, note the exact points cost displayed. For Category 1 properties, this should read 5,000 points per night. Add the room to your cart and proceed — but do not check out yet if your Hyatt account currently has zero balance.

Open a new browser tab and navigate to your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards) or Bilt dashboard. Select "Transfer to Travel Partners" and choose World of Hyatt from the list. Enter the number of points you need (5,000 per night, minimum), confirm your World of Hyatt membership number, and initiate the transfer.

Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant. Note: Sapphire Reserve transfers at 1:1 while Sapphire Preferred transfers at 4:3 (4 UR = 3 Hyatt). Refresh your Hyatt account and your points will be there, ready to use.

Return to your Hyatt browser tab and complete the checkout process. Select "Redeem Points" as your payment method, confirm the points deduction matches what you expected, and finalize the reservation. You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

If your preferred property shows no award availability on your dates, try these workarounds:

Go to hyatt.com and use the "Points + Cash" or "Use Points" search filter. Category 1 properties will display at 5,000 points per night. You can also browse by category directly — look for Hyatt Place and Hyatt House locations in secondary cities and suburban markets.

Always verify that your desired dates show award availability before initiating a transfer from Chase or Bilt. While transfers are instant, confirming availability first ensures you never have orphaned points sitting in your Hyatt account with no immediate use.

Log into your Chase or Bilt account, navigate to the transfer partners section, select World of Hyatt, and transfer the exact number of points needed. Transfers are instant. With a Sapphire Reserve, 5,000 UR points become 5,000 Hyatt points (1:1). With a Sapphire Preferred, you need approximately 6,700 UR points for 5,000 Hyatt points (4:3 ratio). Bilt transfers at 1:1.

Once the points land in your Hyatt account, complete the booking through hyatt.com or the World of Hyatt app. You will pay applicable taxes at checkout (typically $10 to $25 per night) but no additional redemption fees.

Before booking, note the cash rate for the same room and dates. Divide the cash rate by 5,000 to calculate your cents per point. If a room costs $150 per night and you are paying 5,000 points, you are getting 3 cents per point — triple the baseline 1 cent per point cash back value.

Let's make this concrete. You're flying into Nashville for a long weekend — maybe it's a bachelorette party, a music festival, or just a trip you've been putting off. You pull up Hyatt.com and search Nashville for a Friday–Sunday stay (two nights).

Now look at the award column: 5,000 points per night. Two nights: 10,000 points.

Hyatt House properties (also frequently Category 1 or 2) often include a complimentary hot breakfast — eggs, waffles, fruit — served every morning. In some suburban markets, these properties also offer free parking, turning your 5,000-point night into an even stronger value play when you factor in parking rates that might otherwise run $20–$30/night.

This isn't a flashy Park Hyatt penthouse suite. But it's a genuinely comfortable, predictably high-quality stay that you've effectively taken off your cash budget — freeing that $338 for experiences, food, or your investment accounts. That's the ChooseFI mindset applied to travel.

Stack your Hyatt Globalist benefits if you qualify.
