Use the Hyatt free night award from the World of Hyatt Credit Card. The World of Hyatt Credit Card (issued by Chase) comes with an annual free night certificate valid at Category 1–4 properties. Stack this with a paid or points night to effectively get one night free on a multi-night stay — no points required.

Book as far out as you can. The Hyatt booking window opens 395 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer weekends, holiday weekends, major events — inventory at Category 1 properties can thin out. Getting in early locks your room and your rate.

Target Hyatt House properties for family trips. Hyatt House locations frequently feature suite-style rooms with full kitchens, separate living areas, and free hot breakfast included for all guests. A family of four can stay comfortably for 5,000–8,000 points and skip the cost of restaurant breakfasts entirely.

Earn points on the Bilt card on Rent Day. Bilt Rewards runs a bonus promotion on the first of each month — transferring points earned that day at elevated rates. Accumulating Bilt points through rent payments (no transaction fee) is one of the most efficient ways to build a Hyatt balance.

Don't transfer points speculatively. Even though Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant, always confirm your specific dates show award availability before transferring. Points transferred to Hyatt cannot be moved back.

Don't ignore the expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. A single qualifying activity — a points transfer, a stay, a credit card purchase — resets the clock. Set a calendar reminder annually to ensure you don't lose your balance.

Don't overlook Category 2 properties. At 8,000 points per night, Category 2 Hyatts often include urban full-service hotels that provide dramatically more value than the jump in points cost suggests. Once you're comfortable with Category 1 redemptions, explore Category 2 as a natural next step.

This redemption was built for the travel rewards beginner — the person who has accumulated their first 10,000–20,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt points and isn't yet sure if the whole system is real. It's also for the seasoned optimizer who wants a reliable, low-friction redemption they can execute on short notice.

Minimum points needed: 5,000 for a single night. Most people engaging seriously with Chase UR earning will accumulate this through normal spending in a single billing cycle.

In the broader ChooseFI travel strategy, Category 1 Hyatt nights serve as the building blocks — the reliable, repeatable foundation that funds your domestic travel while you accumulate larger balances for the aspirational redemptions.

Create your free World of Hyatt account before you need it — having your membership number ready speeds the transfer process. 2. Start with a one-night stay to build confidence, then scale up. 3. #9007. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#9006. Arudeko transforms discarded wool into paper-like material

Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.

Skilled local artisans initially wove the discarded dyed wool onto a pedal loom, then, using cotton threads, wove strips of recycled paper crafted by local papermakers into the material.

The result is a translucent, flexible textile that can be crafted into diverse objects, from lampshades to decorative headboard panels, room dividers and wall art.

“Through exploring the material’s qualities, we discovered its potential, particularly the way light revealed colours that had been hidden within the paper, almost like a secret waiting to be uncovered,” Arudeko co-founder and CEO Denisse Arnaiz told Dezeen.

“Once the paper was woven, I began observing how it behaved as a textile,” added Arnaiz.

“Its translucency was what ultimately inspired us to explore its use in lighting. However, the material has many other possible applications.”

With Bianni, Arudeko aimed to uncover the hidden value of discarded wool whilst reimagining the ancient material’s ancestral history and “cultural memory”.

“Bianni was born from the idea of giving new life to the leftover wool from our rug and cushion production in Oaxaca,” said Arnaiz. “This wool carries within it the knowledge of the artisans who work with it, as well as the colours of the earth embedded in its fibres.”

Arnaiz explained that the material is made purely from natural materials, with no additives.

“No additives, just natural materials – why mix these fibres?” she said. “Not only for an aesthetic purpose, as wool brings fire resistance to the paper.”

Throughout the process, the studio aimed to minimise water consumption and carbon dioxide production as much as possible. Bianni’s production was also kept local to reduce transport needs whilst supporting the local community.

By working with artisans from rural communities and blending traditional craft knowledge with contemporary design practice, Bianni aims to champion historic crafts whilst fostering long-term community development and economic inclusion.

Other wool projects recently featured on Dezeen include waste-wool cladding designed for retrofits and a collection of rugs with architectural designs.

It's clear that some people are getting tired of the contemporary Disney style. That can be seen in the allegations of Disney same-face syndrome, the disappointment that Hexed doesn't look like its concept art and the perennial controversy over the hybrid live-action remakes, with Moana being the latest flop.

The fatigue was evident at D23 this year. The announcements that generated the most excitement were a return of 2D animation, if only in combination with live action for the nostalgia-heavy TV series in Oswald, and the news that Disney's Clay will look like claymation even if uses CG.

A lot of fans will be happy then to learn that Clay won't be a one off but rather the start of a whole new Disney era after Hexed. The studio's developed a new animation pipeline that will allow it to apply different art styles to 3D models, potentially replacing the realism popularised by Pixar with a unique look for each new movie – and it's all starting with Lilo & Scratch.

Set to show in cinemas alongside Hexed, Lilo & Scratch is the first theatrical short from Walt Disney Animation Studios in five years. Written and directed by Fawn Veerasunthorn and Malcon Pierce, it will see the much-loved blue alien Stitch having to contend with the introduction of a mischievous cat called Scratch. Maia Kealoha voices Lilo, reprising her role from the 2025 live-action film Lilo & Stitch, and Chris Sanders with voice Stitch again.

Like all of the studios' feature animations in the last 15 years, the short was made using computer-generated animation with 3D models, but these are blended with hand-drawn elements to create a hybrid style that looks surprisingly faithful to Lilo & Stitch from 2002.

Disney's VFX supervisor Jeremy Sikorski has said that the new pipeline was developed through experimentation on the previous shorts Paperman and Once Upon a Studio. Pixar is also exploring the same direction, as we saw in the Gatto trailer: environments, characters and sets are modeled and animated in 3D to retain spatial depth, lighting and camera movement, but certain characters and other details are hand drawn.

Disney says about 25% of the backgrounds in Lilo & Scratch are watercolour paintings reused from the original Lilo & Stitch, while more than a dozen new background paintings were created by artists including Tia Kratter and Larry Wu. Some of these were digitally painted in Photoshop to look like watercolour, while others were hand-painted on paper.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Combined with digital backgrounds and set extension, this blend of old and new hand-painted watercolours helped the filmmakers remain faithful to the look of the 2002 feature, Disney says.

In an interview at the Governors Awards in LA on Sunday (see the post by Deadline below), Disney Animation Chief Creative Officer Jared Bush confirmed that all original Disney movies from Clay onwards will use this approach. That doesn't mean that they'll all look like Renaissance-era 2D animation, but that each with have its own "wildly different" look.

Zootopia 3 and Frozen 3 will still look like we would expect, but Hexed may be "the last original in the Disney art style as people know it," he says.

Jared Bush shares updates on ‘Zootopia 3,’ ‘Frozen 3’ and ‘Hexed’ and reveals the new, upcoming animated films at Disney will have “wildly different art styles”: “We’re really going to be pushing into some new areas” | #GovernorsAwards https://t.co/nw16Ci8WoDNovember 16, 2026

The new approach looks like a win for Disney. Despite some success with the live-action The Jungle Book and last year's Lilo & Stitch, the poor reception of Moana, Snow White and Mulan suggests waning interest in the remake formula is waning. Meanwhile, the 3D animation style that once looked so modern is starting to feel dated and generic.

Nostalgic audiences miss 2D animation, while younger audiences want something fresh. It sounds like Disney's new animation pipeline could make both things possible without sacrificing the efficiency that comes with 3D-based CG animation, which makes it much quicker and easier to swap and adjust environments, characters and props compared to traditional hand-drawn 2D, where even a relatively small change might mean having to redraw from scratch.The Disney principles of animation will remain in tact, but in a vast realm new possibilities.

I do wonder though. In ten years time, will people start to feel nostalgic about the much-maligned 3D Disney style?

Hexed will be released on 25 November. Lilo & Scratch will screen before it.

#9004. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

#9003. Rashid Johnson, Christopher Wool, and Dawoud Bey Enter MCA Chicago Collection Through 65-Work Gift

The Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago has received a promised gift of 65 artworks from longtime supporters Jack and Sandra Guthman to mark its 60th anniversary.

The gift from the Chicago-based collectors spans paintings, photography, works on paper, and sculptures, and includes works by Pope.L, Gary Simmons, Andrea Bowers, Christian Marclay, Elle Pérez, and Shinique Smith. The museum said in a release that the selected works were chosen in tandem with the curatorial staff, “taking the MCA’s collecting priorities into serious consideration.” Related Articles Bluhm Family Gives $5 M. to MCA Chicago for Gender Equity Fund, Named After Outgoing Director Outgoing MCA Chicago Director Madeleine Grynsztejn Offers the Consummate Insider's Guide to the Windy City

In its announcement, the MCA Chicago reported that, of the 54 artists represented in the gift, 23 (or 43 percent) are people of color, 19 (or 35 percente) are women, and 13 are entering the collection for the first time, among them Rashid Johnson, Christopher Wool, Dawoud Bey, and Amanda Williams. Johnson’s traveling survey, which opened at the Guggenheim Museum last year, is currently on view at the MCA Chicago; Williams will have a solo show at the museum next year.

“Together, Jack and Sandy have helped shape Chicago’s cultural life through their collecting, advocacy, and longstanding engagement with artists and institutions,” MCA Chicago director Madeleine Grynsztejn said in a statement. “To be entrusted with this tremendous gift is a great honor.”

The Guthmans first donated an artwork to the museum in 1988, and Jack joined the board of trustees the year after. To mark its 50th anniversary in 2016, they donated work by 50 women-identifying photographers, which was the subject of the exhibition “Woman With a Camera.” With the newly donated 65 works, the Guthmans have given a total of 130 works over the past nearly four decades, the largest amount by a single collector in the MCA Chicago’s history.

Jack is an attorney who has worked on several mega-developments in Chicago. He is also the founder and past board chair of the Chicago Architecture Biennial. Sandra worked at IBM from 1965 to 1993, rising from systems engineer to director of marketing for the Midwest. She also served as chief executive and chair of the Chicago-based Polk Bros. Foundation; she is now chair emerita. In addition to the MCA Chicago, they have supported the Art Institute of Chicago, the Hyde Park Art Center, Theaster Gates’s Art Bank, and the Harris Theater for Music and Dance. At the Harris, they sponsored the creation of the Guthman Gallery.

Last month, the MCA Chicago received a $5 million gift from the Bluhm family to endow the Women Artists Initiative, which will provide funds in perpetuity to help the museum achieve its gender equity goals in its programming and collection. Both gifts are meant to honor Grynsztejn, who is stepping down at the end of the year.

“We are fortunate to have the opportunity to donate these works as the MCA marks its 60th anniversary and as Madeleine Grynsztejn steps down after a remarkable tenure as its Pritzker Director,” the Guthmans said in a statement. “We celebrate both the institution and the woman who has lifted it to a where it is today—a Chicago institution now acknowledged as a leader in the world of contemporary art.”

#9002. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

#9000. For Abi Palmer, Chronic Illness Is Like Being an Indoor Cat

“I have been trying so hard to capture the smell of rain for you,” an unseen narrator with a British accent explains in Abi Palmer Invents the Weather (2023), as cats slink across the screen. “But being as I am no god or scientist,” the voice continues, as human hands wring out a cloth soaking in a jar of dirty water, “I am forced to work backward.” Soon, dripping white fabric is seen hanging from twine inside a cardboard box, clumped like a cloud.

This non-god, the artist Abi Palmer, is recreating the weather for her two indoor cats, mixing rainwater with moss and earth. All the while, she muses on how chronic illness keeps her inside, catlike, yet also binds her intricately to meteorological variation. Palmer alludes to the ways joint pain can flare when pressure drops or smoky skies are felt by some in the lungs or in the back of the throat. Related Articles Rashid Johnson, Christopher Wool, and Dawoud Bey Enter MCA Chicago Through 65-Work Gift Artsy and Artnet Acquire First Thursday as Art-Tech Expansion Picks Up Speed

As it happens, Palmer got her start making art in the form of wet white wads. As an “unsupervised child,” as she told me from her London apartment, she’d combine water and tissue into globby sculptures—“blob creatures”—then let them dry. Recently, making massive slug sculptures inspired by the way the species survives by ugliness, she realized how consistent her materials and methods remained. At the University of Cambridge, she studied literature, as is evident in her voice-overs and her two books: Sanitorium (2020) and Slugs: A Manifesto (2024). But soon, she found her hands hurt too much to type—though her muscles were “really bendy” and thus “good at squeezing things into quite unusual shapes,” as she had intuited at a very young age.

It’s not so common, Palmer told me, for cats to live indoors in the UK: Some pet people even consider keeping them inside cruel. But her housing and health situations didn’t allow for her animals to roam freely, never mind that domestic cats kill billions of birds each year. So her video was born of a bit of guilt, an attempt at “navigating the imperfection of the world, but also the magic and beauty of it.” She admitted: “It’s absurd.”

For Palmer, retaining a childlike sense of play is essential. She came to art with little technical training. As she started to receive institutional recognition and awards—she’s been in group shows at the National Museum of Contemporary Art (EMST) in Athens, Goldsmiths in London, EMAP in Seoul, and elsewhere, in addition to receiving the 2025 Heny Moore Foundation Award—she was struck by the haunting sense that she ought to be doing things more “properly.” But she realized: “The moment I start taking things too seriously, it’s a trap.” The external rewards come and go, often without much in the way of remuneration—so it helps to have fun with art. “I take play very seriously,” Palmer said.

Her work attests: In Abi Palmer Invents the Weather she not only elaborately simulates meteorological conditions but shows the video within playful cardboard constructions that she reconfigures for each exhibition: a feline paradise. In a world that tends to address disability and illness in the gravest of tones, Palmer infuses humor. For disabled people, humor can be a survival tactic, a way of putting others at ease with difference—often, not without some resentment. But it is also simply true that life is never one-note.

#8999. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

#8998. Kohler's gut-health tracker clips onto the toilet bowl

American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet, through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health.

Dekoda is designed to be discreet and intuitive, clipping to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

In the emerging toilet-based health tracker market, it is the first device capable of blood detection, which it does through sensors developed at Kohler Health that identify haemoglobin.

The company said the device is particularly useful for older individuals or those with chronic gut illnesses, who need to track their symptoms as part of their disease management programmes.

“When we developed Dekoda, our goal was to give people the tools to listen to their bodies, track meaningful results over time, and take charge of their own wellness journey,” said Kohler Health managing director Nora Tophof.

“It’s important to realise that the human eye is only capable of seeing so much – and trace amounts of blood or other issues are not always apparent,” she continued. “Subtle biological markers, such as microscopic blood or early signs of dehydration, often go unnoticed.”

“Dekoda works quietly behind the scenes to capture those crucial clues, giving people clear, objective data they can use to help shape behaviours or share with their doctor,” Tophof said.

People with dementia often forget to drink or lose the feeling of thirst, while people with gut diseases such as Crohn’s usually need to track their daily bowel symptoms.

A secondary target market is competitive athletes and fitness enthusiasts, who Kohler says can use the hydration data to make training adjustments.

Dekoda is compatible with most toilets. It has a simple flattened capsule shape in gleaming white polycarbonate and attaches to the outside of the rim with an adjustable clamp.

On the other side of the clamp, a customised camera points down into the bowl, using spectroscopy to detect the colour and consistency of urine and stool.

Most of the electronics are contained on the capsule side, along with a magnetic battery that can be removed for charging outside the bathroom. An accompanying fingerprint scanner is designed to be wall-mounted near the toilet so that users can log in and begin their session.

To withstand the bathroom environment, the exterior of the device is made of a polycarbonate that is antibacterial and chemical-resistant, while the mechanical components are made of stainless steel.

A specially trained algorithm analyses the collected data and insights are viewed in the accompanying Kohler Health app. It automatically tracks bathroom routines and identifies trends, while users can also add information about their meals, medications and exercise to add context, and share insights directly with their doctor when they desire.

Users’ data is encrypted as it travels between their devices and Kohler’s systems but decrypted and processed to provide the service.

Kohler Health said Dekoda, which was released in October 2025, is helping destigmatise the collection of gut health-related metrics, which individuals could previously only monitor through test strips or stool samples.

It is part of a small wave of new devices focused on analysing the body’s fluids, from spit to menstrual blood, as wellness technology expands beyond watch-style heart rate monitors and activity trackers.

Normally it's a visual rebrand that gets hackles raised online. A new logo can draw furious ire, as brands like Jaguar and Cracker Barrel have discovered in recent years. Less controversial tends to be copywriting tweaks. But beauty brand Maybelline's 'new' slogan has infuriated me more. Than. Any. Other. Rebrand. This. Year.

“Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline," was one of the most famous jingles on TV for a while. It first debuted in the 1990s (see the original below), and is burned onto the consciousness of countless viewers. But now, in a attempt to remove its so-called "ambiguity", the slogan has been updated. Nay, butchered. One of the best pieces of copywriting, this ain't.

The new slogan reads: "Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline." Yes, "she's" has been changed to a more inclusive "we're". But it's that stuttering punctuation that's bothering me. Why does it suddenly sound like it's being recited by somebody struggling to walk up a hill?

According to Sandrine Jolly, Maybelline's global brand president, the original jingle "was giving ambiguity – it was more of a question". Well, yes. That was rather the point. The word 'Maybe' is, by its very nature, an ambiguous word. Its synonyms include 'possibly' or 'perhaps'. Its entire meaning is uncertainty. You can't change that by giving it a full stop. Trying to remove the ambiguity from a slogan built entirely around ambiguity is a bit like changing Nike's 'Just Do It' to 'Please. Consider. Doing. It.'

And there's nothing wrong with changing 'she' to 'we'. It's a perfectly reasonable attempt at inclusivity, and one that could have been achieved without completely murdering the rhythm. Instead, Maybelline has taken one of the catchiest jingles of all time and made it sound like a hostage reading out a statement. Four sentences where there used to be two. Does that really make for more certainty?

What makes it all so infuriating is that this feels like change for change's sake. The original slogan was clever, memorable and instantly recognisable. The new one needs an entire press release to explain what its punctuation represents. In an era when brands are realising the importance of their heritage branding assets, maybe, just maybe, Maybelline should have left its slogan. Alone.

#8996. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#8995. Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam

Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank

Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.

The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

Located in the heart of Amsterdam, this huge concrete-slab building is in complete contrast to the city’s historic canal houses.

The original architect, Marius Frans Duintjer, had hoped to emulate the modernist works of Mies van der Rohe, but security requirements had resulted in “a fortress with fences, large boulders and armed military police,” according to Mecanoo.

The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.

Mecanoo’s transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.

This allowed the architects to give the building a sense of transparency and openness that was envisioned from the outset, but had never been possible before now.

The project is an exemplar for sustainable renovation, as proven by its nomination for Dezeen Awards 2026.

Removing the cylindrical tower was pivotal, as it allowed space for a new public garden at the heart of the scheme.

This tower was carefully dismantled, allowing many materials to be reused.

Salvaged concrete was used to build a new quay beside the canal, while the rest was donated to social housing projects in the city.

The removal enabled a reorganisation of the ground floor.

The entrance was relocated to Frederiksplein, while floorplates were cut away to reveal the 61-metre-long former vault, which has been transformed into an exhibition gallery.

“The most secretive part of the bank is now its most public,” said Mecanoo.

“Inside the vault, visitors can immerse themselves in exhibitions and interactive games that tell the story of gold, money, the economy and DNB’s core activities.”

The retained structures were newly clad in red ceramic bricks. These incorporate the brown tiles that clad the building previously, with the old tiles crushed for use as pigment.

These combine with new glazing, a Kastenfenster system of ventilated double-glazing with integrated sun shading, which has helped to reduce the building’s day-to-day energy requirements by an estimated 80 per cent.

Inside, the space linking the vault with the courtyard was designed as an indoor street, with seating areas along the edges and auditoriums (one formal, the other informal) at each end.

“Francine Houben’s inspiration came from the vibrant ‘street’ of the central hall in the former Faculty of Architecture building at TU Delft, which was destroyed by fire,” said Mecanoo.

The rest of the building is organised into zones with varying levels of security.

A five-storey atrium organises the semi-public area, which includes a meeting centre and a restaurant overlooking the Singelgracht, while the more secure employee zones are located in both the courtyard building and the tower.

The meeting centre occupies what was previously a double-height cash hall, with distinctive tree-like columns.

The original spiral staircase still stands, alongside a second added by Mecanoo, while custom-designed tables feature integrated lamps.

Timber was used for many of the new surfaces, including a slatted ceiling made from locally felled poplar trees.

Shades of red, blue and orange extend across other surfaces and interior elements, including walls covered in recycled-plastic felt, carpets and furniture.

“The colour scheme is inspired by the vibrant paper currency from the last period of the Dutch guilder,” said Mecanoo.

The interiors are completed by DNB’s collection of artwork, energy-efficient lighting systems and circular planting boxes.

“The renovation transforms De Nederlandsche Bank from a closed fortress into a transparent circular landmark, repurposing the former gold vault as the city’s living room for the public,” concluded Mecanoo.

Other recent projects by the firm include the rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, the tile-clad Villa BW and the book-inspired Macau Central Library.

#8994. Sotheby’s, Blaquier-Arrieta Family Reach Deal With Fischer Heirs, Clearing Way for $180 M. Van Gogh Sale

Sotheby’s has reached an agreement with the heirs of a Jewish publisher who challenged the sale of a $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting last week, clearing the way for the picture to go under the hammer Wednesday night.

The auction house said Tuesday that the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) since 1975, reached a settlement with all the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer. The terms weren’t disclosed, but Sotheby’s confirmed to ARTnews that the agreement resolves the ownership claims and that the painting’s buyer will receive clear title. Related Articles At Sotheby's $378.7 M. Doubleheader, Buyers Take Risks Again, Even as Bidding Drags Yayoi Kusama 'Infinity Net' Painting Sells for $15.1 M. at Sotheby's, Setting a Record

The deal brings an end to a messy public brawl that erupted last Thursday in the pages of the New York Times, just six days before the painting was due to lead Sotheby’s $450 million sale of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection.

As the Times first reported, the Fischer heirs argued that their family had been forced to sell the painting in Amsterdam in 1936 because of financial pressures brought on by Nazi persecution. Their Berlin lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, demanded Sotheby’s withdraw the work from sale unless it could establish that the transaction had been voluntary.

Sotheby’s disputed that account. As ARTnews reported on Sunday the auction house said records from the archives of the art dealer Paul Cassirer showed that the painting sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, or approximately $22,000, in June 1936. Sotheby’s maintained that this was a fair price for a van Gogh at the time, and that the picture had been in Amsterdam for nearly three years before its sale.

The timing of the claim raised eyebrows among several art-market professionals who spoke to ARTnews under the condition of anonymity. Some saw it as a pressure tactic, arriving when Sotheby’s had little time to respond and plenty to lose if the picture was withdrawn. The auction house had guaranteed the work for an undisclosed sum and spent months promoting it as the star of one of the season’s biggest sales.

Judd Grossman, a New York art lawyer who isn’t involved in the dispute, warned that recent changes to the HEAR Act, which governs Nazi-era restitution claims, could encourage more of what he called “gamesmanship by claimants waiting to the very last minute to come forward before seeking their slice of the pie.” (As part of a separate ongoing lawsuit, lawyers for the Republic of Austria, the Albertina Museum, and the Leopold Museum Foundation have labeled the updated HEAR Act unconstitutional.)

Whether the Fischer heirs received any financial compensation under the agreement is unclear. Nor does the settlement establish whether the painting was sold under duress in 1936. In Tuesday’s announcement, Sotheby’s said the agreement recognized both the painting’s complicated history and the persecution suffered by the Fischer family under the Nazis.

The Fischer heirs welcomed the settlement, thanking Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family for what they called a “trusting and fair negotiation” that acknowledged their family’s suffering and honored Gisela Bermann Fischer’s long history of pursuing restitution.

Bermann Fischer, who died in 2014, had previously pursued restitution for artworks lost by her family during the Nazi era. In 2007, she declined to oppose the sale of a Paul Cezanne work that had passed through the same Amsterdam dealer, while expressly reserving her right to challenge other sales.

The Blaquier-Arrieta family also described the settlement positively, saying in a statement it looked forward to “an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”

#8993. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#8991. Reims 502 uses pink palette for "non-referential" commercial building in Mexico

A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.

Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

The studio said the 840-square-metre building was “conceived as an adaptable urban asset” that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.

“Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life,” said the studio.

“Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life.”

Local planning constraints determined the building’s scale, while its “non-referential form” evolved from various design strategies, the studio said.

It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.

Above ground are two open-plan levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

Meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-plan layout to support future commercial activity.

Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

“The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street,” said the studio.

“Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility.”

The pink render that colours the building’s exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.

This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.

According to the studio, the building’s future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as “exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop”.

“This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations,” said Reims 502.

The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

A truly kids-focused 3D printer, which is accessible and simple to use. It's built fairly well, but comes with some key compromises in regard to size and build complexity. It's a fun toy, and a good introduction to 3D printing for younger children.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I was captivated by the idea of a 3D printer designed for children, so I jumped at the chance to let my nine-year-old try the Funbox. She’s wanted a 3D printer for ages. I’ve held out, partly because of the cost and partly because of the inevitable tide of tiny plastic things that would end up around the house.

The Funbox is a compact, good-looking printer made by Ugee. It's fully enclosed for safety, has a clean air filter, is anti-scald and you can create with just a tap via the app. With Christmas coming up, plenty of parents will be hunting for the right option for their kids, so I want to be honest about whether this is it. Does this compare to the best 3D printers?

The external design is delightful. Ugee has nailed the look for kids: it’s cute, it has minimal buttons and fuss, and mine arrived in baby blue. A pack of stickers in the box lets your child decorate it themselves.

The inside is just as accessible. The build plate is easy to put in place and everything is clearly marked to show you how to get started (although we did make a wrong turn by not actually putting the plate in the first time around as you can see above – oops!).

Loading filament is simple, though it can be a bit fiddly for small fingers. It is pretty much plug and play – setup took me about 20 minutes, and my daughter was able to manage the first print pretty much independently with minimal interference, only some instruction. Bear in mind, the build space is small, so this printer is best for smaller prints. You can keep an eye on your print via the camera, which links to the app – my daughter was fascinated by this part.

Designs come from a marketplace in the Funbox app, available for mobile or tablet. It should be simple to use, but it’s glitchy. On our Huion tablet, the ‘start’ button was hidden behind the notch and there was no way to scroll or move the screen to reach it. That forced us onto the mobile app, which wasn’t ideal when I wanted my daughter to use the printer independently, without borrowing my phone.

For the most part, the Funbox worked as expected. My daughter could pick a print and start it herself, and she really enjoyed the process.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The small build volume is the main constraint. Many designs have to be printed in parts and assembled, which is fine if you stick to small prints. For anything more complex, you’ll need to be ready to help with sticking or putting pieces together. It also prints in a single colour at a time.

Most of the toys we printed turned out well, especially single-piece prints with no moving parts. The detail was good, and the results matched what the marketplace listings promised. Highlights include a cat hair comb, a skull and crossbones hair slide and a phone holder, which would hold my phone if it was the right size (note: must check next time).

Functional toys were a different story. We made a couple of fidget toys that couldn’t do their job without breaking. That could be down to the third-party design, or to the filament being too brittle for the purpose. We couldn’t tell which.

That fits what this printer is: a starter machine built for fun, not one that delivers polished, fully functional prints every time.

We haven’t yet tested the AI 3D model builder, which turns your child’s drawing into a printable 3D model. We’ll cover our experience of it in a separate piece.

The Funbox costs $299/£318 but is often on sale for $279/£289. Whether that’s reasonable depends on who you're buying it for.

For my nine-year-old, I’d rather take on the steeper learning curve of a basic ‘grown-up’ printer like the Bambu Lab A1, which I’d expect to give better-quality prints for similar money. It’s less approachable for a child to use alone, but the results would be worth it for her. For a younger child, though, the Funbox’s ease of use and friendly design make a stronger case, and I think they justify the price.

If you want a genuinely child-focused printer, this is a good option. Just be aware you’re trading away print size and complexity.

Choose your designs carefully. Ugee’s own are reliable, but third-party designs from the marketplace are hit and miss.

If your child is at the upper end of the age range (nine to 12), consider a basic printer from one of the adult-focused brands instead. For younger children, the Funbox is the easier fit.

#8989. L-Tyrosine Supplements: Benefits for Your Brain and Body

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

#8988. ways of growing: 20 artists explore plants as design collaborators in lisbon exhibition

20 practitioners utilize bacterial cellulose, living mycelium, plant-dyed textiles, and botanical chemistry to frame plants as active collaborators in design and art.

Haenke edited by christina vergopoulou November 16, 2026 5 min

On view at the Gallery of the Faculty of Fine Arts at the University of Lisbon (FBAUL) through November 28th, 2026, Ways of Growing / Modos de crescer presents works by 20 artists, designers, and researchers examining the intersection of plant biodiversity and material experimentation. Serving as the culmination of the two-year Free Radicals research initiative, led by Haenke (Czech Republic) alongside partners in Portugal, Spain, Armenia, Hungary, and Germany, the exhibition originates from three 2025 field residencies conducted in Galicia’s Courel mountains, a permaculture farm in central Portugal, and northern Armenia’s Lori Mountains.

Rather than treating flora solely as passive raw matter, the exhibited works engage botanical organisms, agricultural byproducts, and local ecologies as active design agents. Material and technical investigations span cyanotypes printed on kombucha-derived bacterial cellulose and toned with plant extracts, bio-composites pairing traditional Portuguese crochet with living mycelium, and textiles woven from chestnut-dyed linen. Additional installations integrate botanical chemistry and digital hardware, including olfactory sculptures formulated from eucalyptus ash and essential oils, plant-based analog film processing, acoustic transmission through organic substrates, and a multimedia system linking historic Armenian herbaria with Raspberry Pi microcomputers. Inaugurated during FBAUL’s 190th anniversary, the exhibition coincides with the release of Free Radicals: Attuning to Plants in Creative Practices (Onomatopee), a publication edited by Sasha Střelcová and Linsey Rendell compiling methodologies from 70 practitioners across design, ecology, and material research.

Elena Falomo’s research-led installation combines field recordings, geographical artefacts and storytelling to question which landscapes are prioritised in responses to climate changeEleonora Edreva’s textile-based poem is woven from vintage linen, chestnut dyes, local language and soundIvana Papić uses ecological fiction to question invasive-species narratives in her experimental video essay imagining a love story between a native chestnut tree and an introduced mimosaAlejandra Díaz-Guerra Acedo’s bio-based textile experiment combines traditional Portuguese crochet with living mycelium, allowing fungi to decompose cotton fabrics buried in contrasting soilsMaria Ilieva’s olfactory compositions trace the lifecycle of eucalyptus from fresh foliage and wildfire to industrial pulp processing and paper productionfood artist and chef Aly Beveridge explores how our proximity to land and ingredients create a bodily intimacy that allows us to reconsider our relationship to foodAdam Kvaček’s performative walk explored the familiar language of recreational tourism to investigate Portugal’s industrial eucalyptus landscapes

name: Ways of Growing / Modos de crescer (Free Radicals)

program: Free Radicals | @freeradicals.space design team: Blanca Allegue, Kač Bártková, Aly Beveridge, Morgane Billuart, Gabriela Carvalho, Alejandra Díaz-Guerra Acedo, Eleonora Edreva, Elena Falomo, Maria Ilieva, Adam Kvaček, Joana Manaia, Jamie McGhee, Ricardo Nugra Madero, Ivana Papić, Béatrice Pépin, Inês Quente, Emilie Rážová, Miguel Tavares, Daria Titova, Yanna Varbanova

lead organization & partners: Haenke (Czech Republic), Quinta das Relvas (Portugal), Fundación Uxío Novoneyra (Spain), Today Art Initiative (Armenia), Pro Progressione (Hungary), Burning Silence (Germany)

#8987. Tant A Temps Design "restores the visual characteristics of Tang architecture" in Chinese cafe

Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.

The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.

The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.

Guided by a “minimum intervention” and “zero damage” renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.

Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets.

Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.

For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.

“The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured,” the studio explained.

“Abandoning the rigid replication of ancient architecture, it extracts and reshapes the spiritual core of Tang and Song aesthetics through a restrained colour palette and minimalist structural language, creating a serene and elegant atmosphere that highly matches the cultural temperament of the Stele Forest.”

An integrated functional island was designed to function as the central bar counter.

All modern utility systems, including air conditioning, water, electricity, lighting and exhausts, were concealed and integrated into the top and bottom of the bar counter.

This is consistent with the studio’s commitment to preserving the heritage building while giving it a contemporary, functional upgrade.

“This forms a functional system that is both independent of the original building structure and seamlessly integrated into the historical environment, setting a new paradigm for the adaptive reuse of similar cultural heritage buildings,” said the studio.

The cafe is part of a 220-square-metre development that also includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop that serves as a history learning centre.

According to Tant A Temps Design, the project has transformed a dormant historical building into an accessible and interactive cultural space.

Led by founder Wei Chen, Tant A Temps Design is an interior design practice based in Xi’an.

Elsewhere in China, Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou and Keiji Ashizawa designed an “open and inviting retail space” in the historic building in Shanghai.
