#8974. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#8973. james bridle and the power of solar, zooplankton, and non-human entities

ancient symbols and microscopic organisms meet contemporary solar technology in an artistic reflection on energy, ecology, and coexistence.

annalise kamegawa November 17, 2026 7 min

Back in 2022, James Bridle—artist, technologist, and author of the book New Dark Age (2018)—created a work called Solar Panels (Radiolaria Series). It was a series of five functional 100W photovoltaic generators, the faces of which were etched with tiny, microscopic zooplankton called Radiolaria. Looking at images of their silica skeletons, enlarged hundreds of times so they are visible to the human eye, reveals a universe of spiky arms, swirling bodies, intricate lattices, and geometric patterns. Juxtaposed with each other, and containing their own advanced modes of capturing energy, Bridle creates a compelling parallel between non-human and human intelligence, and what that could mean for the future of the earth.

Across their writing, installations, and lectures, James Bridle has become known for thinking about the ways that technology, the natural world, and humanity influence each other, with a strong emphasis on understanding ‘intelligence’. They look beyond the popular, mainstream ideas associated with the word, often linked to IQ, large language models, and other forms of reconstructing human thought patterns. In their piece, AI was built on human intelligence. Nature has more to teach, they express the urgency of going beyond this definition, and to learn from the other creatures we share the Earth with.

It is this line of thinking that has underwritten their works with solar panels, water collection systems, and vernacular architecture. Looking back to their 2019 exhibition, Through Other Eyes, which they curated with NeMe Art Centre in Cyprus, an emphasis on more-than-human forms of thinking and creating is evident. Here, they invoked the 1922 writing of Dziga Vertov, in which he describes his fascination with documentation through the lens of a camera. Bridle parallels this with the technologies of the twenty-first century – all the mania, fascination, and consequences – saying that, if we apply these new or different ‘eyes’, those of machines and animals, ‘They might also, if we are open to them, offer us visions of unexpected insight, and startling beauty.’ It is within this vision – trans-species and trans-machine – that Bridle’s work takes form.

Things Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, by James Bridle at Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell AnyoneThings Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, by James Bridle at Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell Anyone

Putting an image of radiolaria on a solar panel conjures ideas about the ability to sustain life and other modalities of using energy generated by natural processes. It calls into question the human need to consume power. Radiolaria, microscopic yet possessing highly advanced skeletal structures, can exist symbiotically with algae that provide them with energy. There is an ancient logic to their existence that can be traced back to the Cambrian. Bridle, in their description of the project, highlights how they were ‘famously illustrated, by the German naturalist Ernst Haeckel, who coined the term “ecology” in 1866.’ The complex structures of these organisms continue to inspire wonder, demonstrating how something so small can be so powerful and complex.

Expanding this logic to the scale of solar panels, a technologically intensive mode of capturing and converting energy from the sun in a way that can power human inventions calls into question the effectiveness of human ‘technology’ when compared to that of the non-human. Here is an incredible invention that can create sustainable energy, a promising alternative to fossil fuels, yet it takes advanced electronics and logistics to achieve what a single-celled organism has been doing for thousands of years. Here, Bridle once again asks us to consider what innovation means, not when we compare it to the span of human history.

In 2023, Bridle expanded on the concept in Things Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, an installation on the archaeological site of Elefsina in Greece, Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell Anyone, just north of Athens. Instead of radiolaria, the images engraved on three 100W solar photovoltaic panels are ‘the wheatsheaf, the poppy, and the calathus,’ which ‘honor the ancient cult of Demeter, and the veneration of the living Earth which she represents.’ Here, the comparison of contemporary power generation with beliefs in ancient deities asks us to question the ways in which energy is created, used, and distributed. Bridle used solar panels to power other works in the installation and the site itself, going on to remark that ‘The technology to do these things, is available to us, and the knowledge of how to do them is not a mystery, nor a secret, but it might require new rituals, and new initiations, to distribute it more widely. This is one of those rituals.’

the poppy that would be inscribed on Bridle’s solar panelssketch of Things Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, an installation on the archaeological site of Elefsina in Greece, Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell Anyone by James Bridle

Ultimately, James Bridle’s solar panel creations reflect a broader vision of posthuman utopias that runs throughout their artistic practice: one in which technology, humanity, and the natural world exist in a more reciprocal relationship. By bringing together ancient natural intelligence and contemporary technologies, Bridle challenges human exceptionalism and conventional ideas of progress. Their work encourages us to look beyond ourselves for models of innovation, recognizing that the natural world already holds sophisticated forms of knowledge. In doing so, they invite us to imagine futures founded on ecological interdependence, collaboration, and coexistence.

Things Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, by James Bridle at Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell AnyoneThings Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, by James Bridle at Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell Anyone | image by Vangelis Gkinis

#8972. Casa Mouda opens Lagos gallery to promote design in Nigeria

Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.

Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.

Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.

Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber said that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.

“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”

The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.

“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.

French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.

Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.

The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones new to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”

Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

#8971. designboom listens: the sounds behind alastair philip wiper’s industrial visions

moving between personal memories, unexpected visual references, and the energy of disco, wiper reveals how music accompanies his work and everyday life.

An album cover encountered in childhood can stay with you for decades. In the case of photographer and creative director Alastair Philip Wiper, the mirrored industrial landscape on The Alan Parsons Project’s Ammonia Avenue became a lasting reference and, eventually, an inspiration for his work. Based in Copenhagen, Wiper turns his camera toward factories, laboratories, scientific equipment, and industrial infrastructures, finding unexpected beauty in the systems people build and the often-absurd ways they operate. His photographs reveal the unexpected visual qualities of places built for function, drawing attention to their symmetry, patterns, and overlooked details.

This week on designboom listens, Wiper shares the music that accompanies his creative moments, moving between disco, jazz, electronic music, and 1980s pop. Some tracks are tied to personal memories, like Cannonball Adderley’s Autumn Leaves, which he played while trying to get his first son to sleep, while others help him find energy or shift his mood. ‘I need something to get me excited and get some energy going. Disco usually does that for me,’ he says of Sister Sledge’s Lost in Music. Kraftwerk’s Radioactivity connects with a book he is currently working on about nuclear technology and culture, while Billy Idol’s Eyes Without a Face echoes some of the more uncanny subjects he has photographed, from robotics to medical and scientific research. Read on for Wiper’s answers and discover the sounds, memories, and visual references behind his practice, then listen to the full playlist below.

What song best captures your creative practice?

Alastair Philip Wiper (APW): Wonderful Life – Black. There are a lot of times when I think I have a wonderful life when working. Not all the time. But then I can just put this song on and I would be back to my wonderful life.

What is the very first track you play to clear the air and get inspired when starting a new project?

APW: Lost in Music – Sister Sledge. I need something to get me excited and get some energy going. Disco usually does that for me.

Is there a song that instantly takes you back to a specific memory or place from your past?

APW: Autumn Leaves – Cannonball Adderly. I played this all the time when I was trying to get my first son off to sleep as a baby, 15 years ago. I would rock him in my arms and bop slowly around the room. Sometimes it worked, a lot of the time it didn’t but I still love it.

What song is stuck in your head right now?

APW: The Captain of Her Heart – Double. Can’t get enough of this 80s beauty.

What is your ultimate 2 AM studio track — the one you secretly know every word to?

APW: Runaround Sue – Dion & The Belmonts. If you want to see me karaoke like an idiot this is probably it.

What song do you put on when you’re stuck and need a breakthrough?

APW:  If You Really Love Me – Stevie Wonder. I’m a massive Stevie Wonder fan and I could have chosen many of his tunes to lift me up, but settled on this. Always puts me in a good mood.

What track is dominating your speakers this week, and is it influencing what you’re making right now? APW: You Always Start it – XXXY. I tend to listen to this tune on repeat for a while, then have a break, then come back to it after a year or so. It’s back this week.

What song helps you slow down and focus on the tiny, quiet details? APW: Within – Daft Punk. I listen to a lot of modern classical like Michael Nyman or Philip Glass when I am trying to focus but want something in the background, but today I decided on this slow one by Daft Punk.

If people were wearing headphones while experiencing your latest work, what one song should be playing? APW:  Radioactivity – Kraftwerk. I’m working on a book about nuclear technology and culture and I love Kraftwerk so it has to be this one.

What is your favorite album cover art? APW:  Island Life – Grace Jones. Jean-Paul Goude is one of my all-time favorite photographers. He was the boyfriend of Grace Jones and was responsible for her whole image around the time she was about the coolest person in the world. All the cool images you have seen of her, looking super sharp, androgynous, robot-like – are down to him. He used to cut up negatives and stitch them together to exaggerate her features – for this image he extended her legs and arms so she seems like a sculpture. Also, The Alan Parsons Project – Ammonia Avenue. I saw this when I was a kid – a photo of some industrial facility which has been mirrored. It stuck with me forever and has been an inspiration for the kind of work I do today.

What track best describes your favorite project you’ve worked on so far? APW: Eyes Without A Face – Billy Idol.  I’ve done a lot of work with sex dolls and robots and cryonics and surgery.

#8970. Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel

Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the new one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.

“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”

Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” said Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio said.

Externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.

It has a rectangular plan, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.

Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.

According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.

“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” said the studio.

“For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”

Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.

Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

#8969. DFA awards 2026 turn regional heritage into global design

grounded in cultural lineage yet operating globally, this year's laureates at the DFA awards 2026 span architecture, material innovation, spatial hospitality, and electric mobility.

mariana rodrigues November 17, 2026 6 min

From sculptural jewelry and spatial architecture to material science and electric mobility, the DFA Awards 2026 place Asian design perspectives at the center of the global conversation. Looking outward while remaining anchored in local sensibilities, this year’s honorees prove that cross-disciplinary craftsmanship and territorial memory are quietly reshaping how the world creates.

Spanning diverse creative practices, the recognized designers merge rigorous technical research with deep cultural intuition, offering tangible solutions and distinct visual languages for an interconnected creative landscape.

Founded in 2003 by the Hong Kong Design Centre, the DFA Awards take root in a city shaped by cross-cultural exchange. Supported by the Cultural and Creative Industries Development Agency, the platform connects regional craft with global markets. From the international stage of Business of Design Week to the DX design hub in Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong operates as an active testbed amplifying Asian perspectives across the wider creative landscape.

The program divides its focus across key pillars of contemporary practice, tracing both lifetime legacies and emerging directions. Sustained contributions to spatial discourse, society, and education in Asia receive the DFA Lifetime Achievement Award (LAA), while the DFA Design Leadership Award (DLA) spotlights leaders who deploy design as a catalyst for viable enterprise. International influence rooted in heritage takes center stage with the DFA World’s Outstanding Chinese Designer (WOCD), honoring creators of Chinese lineage commanding global attention.

Regional collaboration and community stewardship define the DFA Designer of the Year (DOY), complemented by the DFA Asian Design Vanguard (ADV), which champions forward-looking practitioners shaping modern industry. Anchoring the framework, the DFA Design for Asia Awards (DFAA) survey built projects, objects, and visual communication that draw directly from regional cultures to elevate daily life and inform future creative output. Looking toward the next generation, the DFA Hong Kong Young Design Talent Award (YDTA) recognizes emerging practitioners in 2026 focused on environmental sustainability and social responsibility, supporting 18 of them to pursue work or study opportunities abroad and bring global insights back to the local creative scene.

The DFA Lifetime Achievement Award (LAA) honors Yung Ho Chang, founding partner of Atelier Feichang Jianzhu and Dean and Chair Professor of Architecture at the University of Hong Kong. Returning to China after graduating from UC Berkeley, Chang cofounded his studio with Lijia Lu in 1993, merging private spatial experimentation with extensive academic leadership at MIT, Peking University, and the Pritzker Architecture Prize jury. Key works like the Liangzhu Campus for the China Academy of Art, ChunYangTai Arts and Cultural Centre, and Maison de la Chine demonstrate his commitment to joining regional heritage with international architectural logic.

Awarded the DFA Design Leadership Award (DLA), Sonia Cheng proves how mathematical rigor can shape intuitive, atmosphere-driven spaces. Leading both Rosewood Hotel Group and Chow Tai Fook Jewellery Group, the Harvard-educated executive approaches built environments with analytical precision. Since 2011, she has expanded Rosewood to more than 50 locations worldwide, anchoring each property in site-specific craft and local art, while steering Chow Tai Fook through a fresh era of international retail.

The DFA World’s Outstanding Chinese Designer (WOCD) title goes to Hong Kong artist Wallace Chan, recognizing five decades of radical innovation across sculpture and jewelry art. Completely self-taught, Chan merged Chinese philosophy with scientific experimentation, pioneering the three-dimensional Wallace Cut in 1987, specialized clawless settings, and structural titanium sculpture. He expanded his repertoire with Wallace Chan Porcelain, a specialized compound significantly stronger than structural steel. With major acquisitions across the Victoria and Albert Museum and the British Museum, his practice turns esoteric concepts into palpable, light-bending structures.

Named DFA Designer of the Year (DOY), Vector Architects founder Dong Gong has established a compelling spatial language shaped by natural light, local climate, and tectonic clarity. A foreign member of the French Academy of Architecture, Gong transforms everyday landscapes into contemplative civic encounters. His defining works, including the coastal Seashore Library, the Seashore Chapel, the Yangshuo Sugar House hotel conversion, and the Jingyang Camphor Court, showcase an agile balance of raw materiality and site history. With major presentations at MoMA in New York and the Venice Biennale, his practice stands among the most resonant voices in contemporary Asian architecture.

Closing the roster of honorees, the DFA Asian Design Vanguard (ADV) award spotlights Tianyuan Li for recalibrating the contours of electric mobility. Currently heading design at Xiaomi Auto, Li arrived on the global stage as the first Chinese car designer based at BMW headquarters in Munich, steering exterior form on forward-looking projects like the BMW iX and the circular economy concept BMW i Vision Circular. At Xiaomi Auto, he translates digital operating systems into tactile aerodynamic silhouettes, establishing a fluid aesthetic across the Xiaomi SU7 electric sedan, the Xiaomi YU7, and concepts such as the Xiaomi SkyNomad and Xiaomi Vision Gran Turismo. His work demonstrates how vehicle architecture can bridge consumer electronics with high-speed engineering.

Spatial Design takes the lead as the Hong Kong Design Centre announces the 209 winning projects of the DFA Design for Asia Awards 2026. Chosen from entries across 15 economies by a 26-member jury of local and international design figures, the selection spans six design disciplines, with Spatial Design recording the highest proportion of winning entries. The 2026 edition also sees Grand Award winners from Thailand and India return to the top leaderboard for the first time since 2020, pointing to the growing influence of ASEAN design studios.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA shows saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

This step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

Go to britishairways.com, log into (or create) your Executive Club account, and run an Avios award search for the same route and dates. You should see the American Airlines flight(s) appear at 7,500 Avios + a small tax amount — typically $5–$15. If the flight shows up here, you're ready to book.

Once you've confirmed availability, it's time to transfer. Here's what to do based on your points currency:

Important: Only transfer what you need. Points transferred to British Airways cannot be moved back.

Return to BA's award search (refresh if needed), select your American Airlines flight, and complete the booking. You'll pay the Avios from your balance plus the small tax amount with a credit card. You'll receive an American Airlines confirmation number, which you can use at aa.com to manage your reservation, select seats, and add TSA PreCheck or Known Traveler Numbers.

If your ideal date shows no saver inventory, try:

Let's make this concrete. It's mid-October and you want to visit a college friend in Boston for the weekend — flying out of New York's JFK on a Friday evening, returning Sunday afternoon.

You pull up Google Flights. Friday evening nonstops from JFK to BOS? The cheapest is $189. The convenient 6:30 PM departure on American Airlines is $229. Sunday afternoon return is another $199. Round-trip cash cost: $428.

You check aa.com and confirm both flights show saver-level award availability. You open British Airways' site and find:

You transfer 15,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to British Airways — it arrives instantly. You book both flights through BA, receive your AA confirmation numbers, and log into aa.com to select your seats.

If those flights had crept up to $300 each (not unusual around Columbus Day weekend), you'd be looking at 4 cents per point — outstanding for a domestic economy booking.

You're on a standard American Airlines narrow-body — likely a Boeing 737 or Airbus A319. It's economy, which for a 45-minute flight is entirely appropriate. You'll get a beverage service, overhead bin space, and you land at the same gate, use the same terminal, and have the same on-time performance as any other passenger on that plane. The difference is that they paid $229 and you paid $5.60 plus some points that cost you roughly $150 to earn through everyday spending.

That's the FI mindset applied to travel: same experience, radically different cost.

Do This: Book Up to 355 Days Out for Holiday Travel BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance, and American releases its best saver space early. If you're targeting Thanksgiving weekend, Christmas, or a peak summer Friday, set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Award seats on popular routes at peak times go fast.

Do This: Use the Open-Jaw Rule Creatively BA allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. If you're flying into NYC but want to return from a different airport — say JFK inbound and EWR outbound — you may be able to structure this as a single open-jaw award rather than two separate bookings. Worth exploring for multi-city weekend trips.

Avoid This: Booking BA-Operated Flights with This Strategy This cannot be overstated — BA's own flights carry $300–800+ in carrier-imposed surcharges. If you accidentally book a British Airways codeshare or BA-metal flight instead of an American Airlines-operated flight, you'll owe hundreds in fees. Always verify the operating carrier before confirming. Look for 'Operated by American Airlines' in the booking details.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability Points transferred to British Airways are one-way and permanent. Never transfer until you have eyes on the specific flight, date, and saver availability you want. The 30-second search on BA's site before transferring is non-negotiable.

Do This: Keep Your Account Active Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you accumulate Avios for a future trip, make sure to earn or redeem at least a small amount every three years. Even a small shopping portal purchase through the BA Executive Club keeps your balance alive.

Do This: Stack with Other Short Hops Think about recurring trips in your life — quarterly visits to family, annual conferences, weekend trips to a nearby city. This sweet spot isn't just for one redemption; it's a repeatable system. A modest Avios balance of 30,000–45,000 points could cover three to six regional roundtrips per year.

Most U.S. airline loyalty programs use region-based or dynamic pricing for award flights, charging the same number of miles whether you fly 200 miles or 2,000. British Airways uses distance-based pricing instead, which means shorter flights cost dramatically fewer Avios. Since BA is a Oneworld partner with American Airlines, you can use Avios to book AA-operated nonstop domestic flights. The result: a flight that AA might price at 12,500-25,000 miles can be booked for just 7,500 Avios through BA. This is one of the most reliable and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards.

Sign up for a free BA Executive Club account at ba.com. This is where your Avios balance lives and where you will search and book award flights on American Airlines.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant. Only transfer what you need for a specific booking.

On the BA website, search for your route using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for American Airlines-operated nonstop flights. Filter results to find flights coded as AA with available Avios seats.

Confirm the flight is pricing at 7,500 Avios (under 1,151 miles) or 10,000 Avios (1,151-2,000 miles). Check that taxes and fees are the expected $5.60. If prices seem high, try different dates or check that you selected a nonstop flight.

Book the flight and add your AAdvantage number to the reservation so you receive any applicable elite benefits. You will receive a confirmation from British Airways, and the ticket will also appear in your AA account.

Yes. British Airways and American Airlines are both Oneworld alliance members, so you can use BA Avios to book award seats on AA-operated flights. You book directly through the British Airways website (ba.com) and search for AA flight numbers.

Flights under 1,151 miles cost 7,500 Avios each way in economy. Flights between 1,151-2,000 miles cost 10,000 Avios. Flights between 2,001-3,000 miles cost 12,500 Avios. The value proposition is strongest on the shortest flights where the Avios cost is lowest.

Not on domestic American Airlines flights. The typical fee is just $5.60 each way. High fuel surcharges only apply when booking British Airways-operated long-haul flights, not when using Avios on partner airlines like AA domestically.

Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to British Airways Avios. Transfer ratios are 1:1 from Chase, Amex, and Capital One. Transfers are typically instant or within 24 hours.

This sweet spot was practically designed for the ChooseFI beginner — someone who has their first transferable points card (a Chase Sapphire Preferred, an Amex Gold, or a Bilt card) and wants to make a real, tangible redemption without navigating complex routing rules or praying for elusive premium cabin availability.

Minimum to get started: You need at least 7,500 Avios (or transferable points to convert) for a one-way. For a round-trip, 15,000. Most sign-up bonuses — even modest ones — cover multiple round-trips with this sweet spot.

Who this is NOT for: If you're flying coast-to-coast (NYC to LAX is over 2,400 miles — a different, higher Avios tier), this specific pricing won't apply. This sweet spot is purpose-built for short hops under 650 miles. It's also not the move if you already have AA elite status and can snag cheap upgrades — but for the rest of us, it's perfect.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness** — and that rating is fully deserved. Let's be specific about why. The hardest part of most award bookings is finding available seats and navigating confusing partner systems. This one simplifies both: you're searching a major U.S. airline's (AA) domestic saver inventory, which is widely available on popular short-haul routes year-round. You're not hunting for a specific aircraft with lie-flat seats or hoping a single partner releases one business class seat. Domestic economy saver space is genuinely accessible. The booking process itself is two websites: aa.com to check availability, britishairways.com to book. Neither requires a phone call, neither has complicated routing rules for simple one-way or round-trip domestic bookings, and the transfer from Chase or Amex is instant. **The three things to get right:** 1. **Confirm saver availability on AA before transferring** — This habit protects you from the only real risk (irreversible point transfers). 2. **Verify the operating carrier is American Airlines, not British Airways** — One glance at 'Operated by' in the booking details handles this. 3. **Keep your BA Executive Club account active** — Set a reminder to log in or earn at least once every 36 months so your Avios don't expire. That's genuinely the whole checklist. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is the redemption to start with. You'll build the muscle memory — search, confirm, transfer, book — in about 20 minutes, and you'll have a nearly free flight to show for it. Welcome to travel rewards.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Using British Airways Avios for short domestic nonstop flights on American Airlines is one of the most practical and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards. At just 7,500 Avios each way with $5.60 in fees, it dramatically undercuts what AA charges through its own program. With four major transfer partners feeding BA Avios, this sweet spot is accessible from virtually any points-earning strategy. Whether you are booking a quick NYC-Chicago hop or an LA-San Francisco shuttle, BA Avios should be your first look for short-haul domestic flights.

#8967. Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead

Sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

“I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” said McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

“At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” said McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”

“If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

“It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” said McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

“So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “

While the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

“There’ll be a few modifications,” he said. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “important part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

“There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” said McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”

#8966. Photos reveal scale of Trump’s White House ballroom, drawing criticism

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump announced the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”

It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

Architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

“[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s West Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion said it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

The administration has also floated plans to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

#8965. john pawson sets white ribbon staircase against 18th century baroque portal at the madrid EDITION

ian schrager pairs john pawson’s refined minimalism with françois champsaur’s artistry inside madrid’s former monte de piedad bank, converted by OAB and ruiz-larrea into the hotel brand's second spanish address.

sofia lekka angelopoulou November 17, 2026 6 min

John Pawson takes his cue at The Madrid EDITION hotel from an eighteenth-century baroque portal he inherited. Spanish architect Pedro de Ribera carved it for the chapel of the Monte de Piedad, the charitable pawnshop that Francisco Piquer, chaplain of the Descalzas Reales convent across the square, founded in 1702 to lend to the poor. The savings bank that grew out of that pawnshop demolished the chapel in the 1960s and kept the portal, resetting it on the face of its new office building.

It is this building that OAB (Office of Architecture in Barcelona) and Ruiz-Larrea convert into the brand’s second Spanish address after the Barcelona EDITION of 2018, with interiors by Pawson and Paris-based François Champsaur, all orchestrated under the eye of Ian Schrager. Pawson names the challenges of the inherited architecture as the project’s defining inspiration, and his response turns on a lobby with two very different entry experiences: a lower entrance clad in dark baroque timber around a sculptural white staircase, and a second entrance through the portal itself on the historic Plaza de las Descalzas.

From the historic square, the Madrid EDITION building reads as clean-lined and almost reticent, its single flourish the carved decorative portal that frames the entrance. Around the corner, a copper canopy and a curtain of greenery announce the main entry, with Pawson’s white sculptural spiral staircase, free of visible handrails, coiling up toward the lobby where the two entrances meet.

There, the Lobby Bar sits beneath an undulating plane that softens the room’s proportions, lit almost entirely indirectly, with spotlights reserved for the pieces worth looking at: reissued Jean-Michel Frank sofas and armchairs, recycled bronze stools cast by Maison Intègre at its foundry in Ouagadougou, rope-wrapped chairs by Christian Astuguevieille, and a pool table that Emmanuel Levet Stenne cut from a single slab of white Bianco Neve marble. A hand-scalloped copper bar runs along one side with a backlit caged bottle display behind it, and a U-shaped sofa with backlit shelves anchors the middle of the room.

In a corner off the lobby, the Punch Room goes darker still, with dark oak panels, a basalt stone fireplace, gray pony hair armchairs, a brushed copper bar and a bronze-polished mirror by Paris studio Garnier & Linker.

Ribera’s carving does not stay outside, it reappears in the double-height dining room of the all-day Italian restaurant, which enters directly through the portal from the plaza. There, dark oak wall panels take their pattern from the stonework a few meters away, hung with two alabaster and plaster pendants by Levet Stenne. The room opens into a lounge along a long green marble bar laid over white oak floors, then into a lighter third area of white marble tables.

The motif travels upstairs too, in each of the hotel’s 200 guest rooms, where custom made plaster headboards are shaped after the elaborate form of the hotel’s baroque portal. The rooms’ interiors carry the contrast of light and darkness down to the threshold. An entrance panelled in dark oak gives onto a light-filled palette of whites and creams, with custom furnishings and the natural textures of linen, limestone and timber forming what the hotel calls an honest and discreet canvas for the detail work.

‘I am very proud of this project,’ says Schrager, the visionary pioneer of the boutique and lifestyle hotel brand. ‘Not a single detail has been overlooked and the finished product has created a unique and magical concept.’

23 of the 200 rooms are suites, while two penthouses take the west side of the fourth floor for the sunset, arranged as duplexes with the bedrooms upstairs and the living space and a butler’s kitchen below. The larger of them, the Madrid Penthouse, opens onto a panoramic terrace with its own infinity pool set in greenery, furnished with a leather and wood daybed by BassamFellows and an eight-seat travertine dining table on lacquered metal feet.

The fourth-floor rooftop holds the property’s showpiece: the largest infinity pool built on the roof of an existing building in Madrid, edged by 25 sunbeds and five cabanas, with the city’s terracotta rooftops unrolling toward the sunset. The rooftop is also home to Oroya, the Peruvian restaurant of chef Diego Muñoz, set in a greenhouse-like dining room of blackened steel, climbing plants and colored glass. Outside, a vine-covered pergola shades the restaurant’s terrace, where a fireplace, a bleached teak bar and a long oak table offer guests a relaxed, convivial atmosphere to enjoy lazy lunches or afternoon cocktails.

#8964. Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” said the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

“What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges said. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” said the master jury.

“The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

First, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

“Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers

Baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes users away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” said the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges said.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic company, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” said the judges.

“The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”

Looking ahead, the judges said “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

“Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they said. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” said the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

“This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

“This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges said. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

“This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges said. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

“This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete

The project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” said the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

“As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”

#8963. ukrainian artists reimagine historic tree of life mosaic with 5,000 reclaimed fragments

at COP31 in antalya, an interactive installation invites visitors to assemble a colorful artwork celebrating cultural memory, creativity and collective renewal.

A historic Ukrainian mosaic is finding a new life at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, where thousands of reclaimed fragments come together in an interactive installation celebrating art, memory, and collective creativity. Titled Tree of Life, the project reimagines a celebrated 1967 artwork from Mariupol through a contemporary composition made from approximately 5,000 pieces of glass, ceramics, tiles, and recovered construction materials. Initiated by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Ukraine, the installation was developed by artists from the Monument-ta mosaic studio and the Alla Horska and Viktor Zaretskyi Foundation, with financial support from the Government of Japan.

The project draws inspiration from a monumental mosaic created in Mariupol in 1967 by a group of Ukrainian artists led by Alla Horska. Known for its vibrant colors, organic forms, and symbolic imagery, the original work became an important example of Ukrainian monumental art. Concealed behind a brick wall in the 1970s, the composition was rediscovered in 2008, bringing renewed attention to its artistic and cultural significance. Nearly six decades after its creation, its distinctive visual language has been reinterpreted for an international audience, connecting artistic heritage with contemporary ideas of material reuse and collective participation.

The contemporary Tree of Life combines approximately 5,000 individual fragments, including 55 kilograms of construction materials recovered from buildings in the Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Kharkiv regions. Rather than using pieces from the original Mariupol mural, the artists have created an entirely new composition inspired by its forms and symbolism. Measuring approximately 1.25 meters high and 2.1 meters wide, the installation consists of 51 individual elements arranged to form the outline of Ukraine, with an additional branch extending toward Crimea. Colorful botanical patterns and decorative details reference the artistic vocabulary of the 1967 mosaic while introducing a new visual identity.

A team of ten artists spent 84 hours assembling the composition, developing a system of 205 magnets that allows its individual elements to be attached and repositioned. Each section weighs between one and two kilograms, making the artwork both modular and interactive. Visitors to the Ukrainian Pavilion are invited to place the pieces themselves, gradually completing the image through a shared process. What might have been a conventional exhibition piece becomes an invitation to participate, with the audience taking an active role in bringing the composition together. The result is an artwork that continues to evolve through the gestures of those who encounter it.

Beyond its artistic references, Tree of Life explores the creative possibilities of material recovery and circular design. By incorporating existing glass, ceramics, and construction materials into a new composition, the project demonstrates how everyday fragments can acquire fresh cultural and aesthetic value. The approach also connects the installation with broader conversations at COP31 surrounding resource efficiency, sustainable construction, and the circular economy. Here, reuse is not presented as a purely technical process, but as an opportunity for experimentation and expression, where materials carry stories from one context into another.

Presented as part of the Ukrainian Pavilion’s programme, Ukraine is the Solution, the installation brings together cultural heritage, contemporary craftsmanship, and environmental awareness. Its interactive format encourages visitors to consider reconstruction as a collective creative process, while celebrating the enduring relevance of Ukrainian artistic traditions. Rather than simply reproducing a historic image, the artists have developed a new work that invites participation and reinterpretation. At a conference dedicated to imagining more sustainable futures, Tree of Life offers a particularly tangible proposition: sometimes renewal begins with what is already there.

artists: Monument-ta mosaic studio and Alla Horska and Viktor Zaretskyi Foundation

artistic concept: Tetiana Tadai and Olena Zaretska

location: Ukrainian Pavilion, COP31, Antalya, Turkey
